順天府鄉試錄序
皇上御極之十年，秋八月，順天府復當鄉試士。府尹臣國彥、府丞臣煥職在提調，以例請。上命諭德臣賡、侍講臣世能為考試官。既陛辭入院，則集諸同考官進士臣錫類，教授臣正蒙、臣台卿，學正臣仲廉、臣懋賞，教諭臣應箕、臣問禮、臣天秩，訓導臣思謙、臣密、臣觀德，用禮官所條上科指，相與必誠惟謹；而御史臣廷試、臣祥暨臣雷士
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination

In the eighth month of autumn of the tenth year of His Majesty's reign, it was once again time for Shuntian Prefecture to examine scholars in the Provincial Examination. Prefect (fuyin) Your Servant Guoyan 國彥 and Vice Prefect (fucheng) Your Servant Huan 煥, whose official duties were to serve as Proctors, petitioned in accordance with precedent. His Majesty commanded Admonisher (yude) Your Servant Geng 賡 and Expositor-in-Waiting (shijiang) Your Servant Shineng 世能 to serve as Examiners. Once they had taken leave of the throne and entered the examination compound, they assembled all the Associate Examiners—Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) Your Servant Xilei 錫類; Prefectural Directors of Studies (jiaoshou) Your Servant Zhengmeng 正蒙 and Your Servant Taiqing 台卿; Subprefectural Directors of Studies (xuezheng) Your Servant Zhonglian 仲廉 and Your Servant Maoshang 懋賞; District Directors of Studies (jiaoyu) Your Servant Yingji 應箕, Your Servant Wenli 問禮, and Your Servant Tianzhi 天秩; and Assistant Directors of Studies (xundao) Your Servant Siqian 思謙, Your Servant Mi 密, and Your Servant Guande 觀德—and, applying the examination guidelines itemized and submitted by the officials of the Ministry of Rites, pledged to one another to act with utmost sincerity and prudence; while Investigating Censors (yushi) Your Servant Tingshi 廷試 and Your Servant Xiang 祥, together with Your Servants Lei Shi…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
楨臣洪聲遠約束於闈內外
者亦惟是科指是飭乃合諸
曹六館及提學御史臣朱璉
所選士四千二百餘人三試
之遵
制額取百三十五人幷錄其文
以
===
獻臣賡謹序其端曰夫世登降
豈不在士習哉夫士非患夫
僕邀罷駑役役榮利之能易
世也惟世所稱超乘之士洸
洋自恣輯非經之語學不徵
之事跳而匿其短游大人以
成其名使聽之若失而走之

以
===
獻臣賡謹序其端曰夫世登降
豈不在士習哉夫士非患夫
僕遫罷駑役役榮利之能易
世也惟世所稱趨衆之士洸
洋自恣輯非經之語學不徵
之事跳而匿其短游大人以
成其名使聽之若失而走之
punctuated: 楨、臣洪聲遠約束於闈內外者，亦惟是科指是飭。乃合諸曹、六館及提學御史臣朱璉所選士四千二百餘人三試之，遵制額取百三十五人，幷錄其文以獻。臣賡謹序其端曰：夫世登降，豈不在士習哉？夫士非患夫僕邀罷駑、役役榮利之能易世也。惟世所稱超乘之士，洸洋自恣，輯非經之語，學不徵之事，跳而匿其短，游大人以成其名，使聽之若失而走之
translation_en:
…[Lei Shi]zhen 雷士楨 and Your Servant Hong Shengyuan 洪聲遠—who maintained discipline inside and outside the examination compound—likewise strictly enforced only these examination guidelines. Thereupon, we gathered the more than 4,200 scholars selected by the various government offices, the Six Halls of the Directorate of Education, and the Education-Intendant Censor Your Servant Zhu Lian 朱璉, and tested them in three sessions. In accordance with the imperially decreed quota, we selected 135 men, and we have also recorded their essays to present to the throne.

Your Servant [Shen] Geng 沈賡 respectfully writes by way of a preface at the beginning of this record: Does not the rise and fall of the age lie in the habits of its scholars? Yet as for scholars, the worry is not that those who are petty, worn-out, and mediocre, slaving away after glory and profit, are capable of changing the world. Rather, it is when those whom the world acclaims as transcendent talents—boundless and unrestrained in their self-indulgence—compile uncanonical phrases, study unverified matters, leap about to conceal their shortcomings, and court great men in order to make their names, causing those who hear them to be as though dazed and those who flock to…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
者如騖蓋天下始病也何者
榮利之習卑卑爾自好者不
屑而世所稱超乘之士衆耳
是寄化肖甚速其禍不至於
中膏肓壞敎化不止是以君
子患之也周之衰妾婦之行
接迹於道孟氏顧猶末減而
===
窮詰於邪說詖行彼談天炙
輠閃倏狡獪真榛蕪不可共
於途檮杌不可共於世哉我
國家彌綸素業陶埴章縫士生
成弘以前者其文典實雅馴
已盡不復語持議不越於中
庸無甚高論試之於天下非
alt_text:
者如鶩蓋天下始病也何者
榮利之習畢畢爾自好者不
屑而世所稱超乘之士衆耳
是寄化肖甚速其禍不至於
中膏肓壞教化不止是以君
子患之也周之衰妻婦之行
接迹於道孟氏顧猶未減而
===
窮詰於邪說詖行彼誠天炙
輠閎倏佼獪貞榛蕪不可共
於逵檮杌不可共於世哉我
國家彌綸素業陶埴章縫士生
成弘以前者其文典實雅馴
巳盡不復語持議不越於中
庸無甚高論試之於天下非
punctuated: 者如騖，蓋天下始病也。何者？榮利之習，卑卑爾，自好者不屑；而世所稱超乘之士，衆耳是寄，化肖甚速，其禍不至於中膏肓、壞敎化不止，是以君子患之也。周之衰，妾婦之行接迹於道，孟氏顧猶末減，而窮詰於邪說詖行。彼談天炙輠、閃倏狡獪，真榛蕪不可共於途、檮杌不可共於世哉！我國家彌綸素業，陶埴章縫，士生成、弘以前者，其文典實雅馴，已盡不復語，持議不越於中庸，無甚高論；試之於天下，非
translation_en: …those who flock to them are like stampeding horses; only then does the Empire truly fall ill. Why is this? The habit of seeking glory and profit is merely base, so those with self-respect disdain it; whereas toward those whom the world calls transcendent scholars, the ears of the multitude are drawn, and people transform to resemble them with great speed. The disaster they cause does not stop until it strikes the vital organs and ruins moral instruction; for this reason, the gentleman worries about them. In the decline of the Zhou, the conduct of concubines and wives followed one after another along the way, yet Mencius treated that more lightly, while exhaustively interrogating heretical doctrines and biased actions. Were those who "discoursed on the heavens" and "spouted oil like a greased axle," flashing and deceitful, truly like brambles and weeds with which one could not share the road, or like the Taowu monster with which one could not share the world? Our Dynasty comprehensively orders its foundational enterprise and molds its Confucian scholars. Scholars born before the Chenghua (1465–1487) and Hongzhi (1488–1505) eras wrote prose that was canonical, substantive, elegant, and refined; once their meaning was fully expressed, they said no more, and the views they upheld did not overstep the Constant Mean, containing no excessively lofty discourses. When tested in the governance of the Empire, unless…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
艱難盤錯率兢兢守尺寸無
奇舉也故士鮮縹囊之名而
國家實受其福迨其後也崇詭
灧而卑體要喜豪舉而厭繩
墨捷摩揣而賤循守原夫才
智豈復賢於先哲而名則過
之譬之醇焉日醨日漓蓋士
為名高而天下之神理苶然
瘁矣迹之不知所從而舉世
譁讙嚮之至於今益烈吁可
誡也我
皇上統一道眞續三五緒卽博雅
好文圖史不輟目而
淵衷所孜孜者惟收心養性之學
alt_text:
鄞鄞盤錯率兢兢守尺寸無
奇舉也故士鮮縹囊之名而
國家實受其福迨其後也崇詭
鑿而畢體要喜豪舉而厭繩
墨捷摩揣而賤循守原夫才
智豈復賢於先哲而名則過
之譬之醇焉日漓日益士
===
爲名高而天下之神理蕪然
瘁矣迹之不知所從而舉世
譁讙嚮之至於今益烈吁可
誠也我
皇上統一道眞續三五緒即博雅
好文圖史不輟目而
淵衷所孜孜者惟收心養性之學
punctuated: 艱難盤錯，率兢兢守尺寸，無奇舉也。故士鮮縹囊之名，而國家實受其福。迨其後也，崇詭灧而卑體要，喜豪舉而厭繩墨，捷摩揣而賤循守。原夫才智，豈復賢於先哲？而名則過之。譬之醇焉，日醨日漓。蓋士為名高，而天下之神理苶然瘁矣。迹之不知所從，而舉世譁讙嚮之，至於今益烈，吁，可誡也！我皇上統一道眞，續三、五緒，卽博雅好文，圖史不輟目，而淵衷所孜孜者，惟收心養性之學，
translation_en: … confronting knotty and intricate difficulties, they generally abided cautiously by established standards without making any flashy moves. Thus scholars rarely won fame for literary brilliance, yet the state truly enjoyed the blessings of their service. In later times, however, men came to exalt the bizarre and flamboyant while despising substance and essentials; they delighted in grandiose gestures while tiring of rules and measures; they prided themselves on nimble speculation while looking down on steady adherence to duty. If we trace their actual talents and wisdom, how could they possibly surpass the worthies of earlier generations? Yet their reputations exceeded them. It is like pure wine becoming thinner and more diluted day by day. Indeed, as scholars pursued lofty reputations, the vital spirit and moral order of the realm grew exhausted and worn down. If one traces this trend, one knows not whence it arose, yet the whole world clamored after it in noisy admiration, and down to the present day it has grown ever more intense—alas, how worthy of warning this is! Our Augustus and Sovereign unites the true Way and continues the heritage of the Three Kings and Five Emperors. Even though he is broadly learned and fond of letters, never taking his eyes off charts and histories, what his profound mind tirelessly devotes itself to is solely the learning of gathering in the mind and nourishing one's nature; …

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
齋居之製可誦已頃復
深詔天下程先民還爾雅視昔加
嚴焉
聖修若彼
廣厲若此而四方不應於桴鼓
臣不信也矧都人士耳目最
親者哉臣幸執經史曰侍
===
上左右嘗稱引王旦李沆不用浮
薄語為
上分明之賴
聖明不忌切慤若有當焉脫今日
不免以若人進是臣棄生平
愧前哲背成言篩
主聽罪大不細故受

臣不信也矧都人士耳目最
親者哉臣幸執經史口手
===
上左右嘗稱引王旦李沆□用沆
薄語爲
上分明之賴
聖明不忌切懿若有當焉脫令日
不免以若人進是臣棄生平
愧前哲背成言飾
主聽罪大不細故受
punctuated: 齋居之製，可誦已。頃復深詔天下，程先民，還爾雅，視昔加嚴焉。聖修若彼，廣厲若此，而四方不應於桴鼓，臣不信也；矧都人士耳目最親者哉！臣幸執經史，曰侍上左右，嘗稱引王旦、李沆不用浮薄語為上分明之。賴聖明不忌切慤，若有當焉。脫今日不免以若人進，是臣棄生平、愧前哲、背成言、篩主聽，罪大不細。故受
translation_en: …the compositions written during his fasts and retreats can be recited as proof of this. Recently, he has again issued a profound decree to the empire to take the ancient worthies as a standard and return to refined elegance, making the requirements even stricter than before. With His Majesty's sage self-cultivation being such as that, and his broad encouragement of scholars being such as this, that the four quarters should not respond like a drum to a drumstick—your servant does not believe it; how much more so the scholars of the capital, whose eyes and ears are closest to the throne! Your servant has been fortunate enough to hold the Classics and Histories in daily attendance[?] at His Majesty's side, and once cited the words of Wang Dan 王旦 and Li Hang 李沆 on not employing superficial and frivolous men, explaining them clearly for His Majesty. Relying on His Sacred Brilliance not taking offense at earnest and blunt words, it seemed they met with his approval. Should I today fail to avoid advancing such superficial men, then your servant would be abandoning his lifelong principles, shaming those former wise statesmen, going back on his own established words, and deceiving[?] the sovereign's hearing—a crime great and by no means trivial. Therefore, since receiving…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
任以來凜凜日夕誓於言語文字
之外得士先察其朴忠而後
求其才敏毋令使天下以臣
爲嚆矢也屠龍天下之絕伎
也學之三年伎成而無所用
之夫使無所用之而天下之
學屠龍者寡矣劉劭論人物
===
先平淡後聰明使平淡與聰
明之士絜眉宇而較脣吻何
啻謝不敏然而先之蓋平無
傾必爲正大淡無涅必爲光
明質量中和變化應節譬無
味而五味得和焉故足多也
臣願諸士徵臣於劉劭也抑
alt_text:
何以來廩廩日夕誓於言語文字
之外得士先察其朴忠而後
求其才敏毋令使天下以臣
爲蒿矢也屠龍天下之絕伎
也舉之三年伎成而無所用
之夫使無所用之而天下之
學屠龍者寡矣劉勰於人□
===
先平淡後聰明使平淡與聰
明之士叢眉宇而較唇吻何
啻謝不敏然而先之蓋平無
傾必爲正大淡無涅必爲光
明質量中和變化應節譬無
味而五味得和焉故足多也
臣顥諸士徵臣於劉劭也抑
punctuated: 任以來，凜凜日夕，誓於言語文字之外得士，先察其朴忠，而後求其才敏，毋令使天下以臣爲嚆矢也。屠龍，天下之絕伎也；學之三年，伎成而無所用之。夫使無所用之，而天下之學屠龍者寡矣。劉劭論人物，先平淡，後聰明。使平淡與聰明之士絜眉宇而較脣吻，何啻謝不敏？然而先之，蓋平無傾，必爲正大；淡無涅，必爲光明。質量中和，變化應節，譬無味而五味得和焉，故足多也。臣願諸士徵臣於劉劭也。抑
translation_en: … taking up this commission, I have been filled with awe day and night, vowing to find men of worth beyond mere speech and writing—first examining their unadorned loyalty, and only afterward seeking their talent and quickness—so as not to let the empire take me as the starting point of a bad trend. Slaying dragons is the most consummate skill in the world; yet if one studies it for three years and perfects the skill, there is nowhere to use it. Now, if it is rendered useless, then those in the world who study dragon-slaying will become few indeed. When Liu Shao 劉劭 discussed human character, he placed the even and bland before the clever and brilliant. If one were to make an even and bland scholar and a clever and brilliant scholar measure their countenances and compare their eloquence, would the former not merely beg off for lack of ability? Yet he placed the even and bland first, because what is even does not tilt, and so must be upright and great; what is bland cannot be stained black, and so must be bright and pure. When substance and measure are balanced and harmonious, transforming in response to the proper rhythms, it is like that which has no flavor of its own yet enables the five flavors to achieve harmony; therefore, it is worthy of high esteem. I wish that all you scholars would verify my words by those of Liu Shao. Moreover, …

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
微獨劭虞廷九德不外中和
皇極敷言要歸正直夫昔人
謂虞周之際道在皐陶箕子
矣而其言若此故臣願諸士
徵臣於虞周也且吾成弘以
前士咸用此轍稱先進云故
臣又願諸士徵臣於成弘以
===
勗諸士猶理王旦李沆之故
臣非臆說庶幾又萬有一之
當於
聖心也
左春坊左諭德兼翰林院侍
讀朱賡謹序
alt_text:
徽獨卲虞廷九德不外中和
皇極敷言要歸正直夫昔人
誚虞周之際道在皐陶箕子
矣而其言若此故臣願諸士
徵臣於虞周也且吾戚弘以
前士咸丙此轍稱先進故
臣又願諸士徵臣於此
===
勗諸士猶理王旦李沆
臣非臆說庶幾又萬有之
當於
聖心也
左春坊左諭德兼翰林院侍
讀朱賡謹序
punctuated:
微獨劭，虞廷九德，不外中和；皇極敷言，要歸正直。夫昔人謂虞、周之際，道在皐陶、箕子矣，而其言若此，故臣願諸士徵臣於虞、周也。且吾成、弘以前，士咸用此轍，稱先進云，故臣又願諸士徵臣於成、弘以勗諸士，猶理王旦、李沆之故。臣非臆說，庶幾又萬有一之當於聖心也。
左春坊左諭德兼翰林院侍讀朱賡謹序。
translation_en:
…Not only Liu Shao: the Nine Virtues of the court of Yu were nothing other than centrality and harmony, and the broadcast of words on the August Ultimate came down in essence to uprightness and rectitude. Now, men of the past said that during the eras of Yu and Zhou, the Way rested with Gao Yao 皐陶 and Jizi 箕子; yet their words were like this. Therefore, your servant wishes the gentlemen to verify my words against the eras of Yu and Zhou. Moreover, prior to our Chenghua and Hongzhi reigns, scholars all followed this track and were praised as the predecessors; therefore, your servant further wishes the gentlemen to verify my words against the Chenghua and Hongzhi eras so as to encourage the gentlemen, just like reviving the precedents of Wang Dan 王旦 and Li Hang 李沆. Your servant is not speaking from mere conjecture; perhaps there may even be one chance in ten thousand that this accords with the Sacred Mind.

Respectfully prefaced by Zhu Geng 朱賡, Left Admonisher of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent concurrently serving as Expositor-in-Waiting in the Hanlin Academy.

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:

punctuated:
第壹場

四書
子曰：「中庸之爲德也，其至矣乎！民鮮久矣。」
去讒遠色，賤貨而貴德，所以勸賢也。
堯、舜之治天下，豈無所用其心哉？

易
《象》曰：「厥孚交如」，信以發志也；「威如之吉」，易而无備也。
《彖》曰：鼎，象也。以木巽火，亨飪也。聖人亨以享上帝，而大亨以養聖賢。巽而耳目聰明，柔進而上行，得中而應乎剛，是以元亨。
言行，君子之所以動天地也，可不慎乎！
震爲雷，爲龍。

書
禹曰：「於！帝念哉！德惟善政，政在養民。水、火、金、木、土、穀，惟修；正德、利用、厚生，惟和。九功惟叙，九叙惟歌。戒之用休，董之用威，
translation_en:
First Session

The Four Books
The Master said: "Supreme indeed is the Mean as a moral virtue! It has long been rare among the people."
Dispelling slanderers and keeping beauty at a distance, scorning wealth and prizing virtue—this is the way to encourage the worthy.
In ruling the world, did Yao and Shun have nothing upon which they applied their minds?

Book of Changes (Yi)
The Commentary on the Images (Xiang) says: "'His sincerity is reciprocated' means that his trustworthiness inspires the wills of others; 'the good fortune of his majesty' comes from being easygoing and without artifice."
The Commentary on the Decision (Tuan) says: "The Cauldron (Ding) is an image. Putting wood beneath fire is cooking. The sage cooks in order to make offerings to the Lord on High, and cooks on a grand scale in order to nourish the sages and worthies. Through compliance, the ears and eyes become acute and clear; the yielding advances and moves upward, attaining the center and responding to the firm; therefore there is supreme success."
Words and deeds are that whereby the noble man moves heaven and earth—how could he not be cautious?
Zhen is thunder, and is the dragon.

Book of Documents (Shu)
Yu said: "Oh! May the Sovereign bear this in mind! Virtue lies in good governance, and governance lies in nourishing the people. Water, fire, metal, wood, earth, and grain must be regulated; the rectification of virtue, the utilization of resources, and the enrichment of livelihood must be harmonized. When the nine endeavors are ordered, those nine ordered endeavors may be celebrated in song. Admonish them with felicitation, supervise them with majesty, …"

punctuated: 又建制立法，圖惟億萬年之安，樞機品式，古今罕儷。創守兼善，無論漢、唐、宋，即湯、武讓烈矣。聖德神功，在《大明日曆》、《聖政記》，當時儒臣親見其盛而恭序之，一謂其規摹宏遠，一謂其綱舉目備，創守之績具矣，其前後艱難之慮，可指言之歟？皇上懋篤聖修，顧諟祖德，頃因講讀《訓錄》，而首舉《創業艱難》一編，循環紬繹，於十載百戰之勞、三紀經營之略，宛在聖心，夙宵圖理，益厪厪焉。守成致盛，真在今日矣。諸生亦能楊厲而仰佐萬分一歟？有一可采，將以上聞，毋略。
translation_en:
…further established institutions and enacted laws, planning for the security of hundreds of millions of years; the pivotal mechanisms and regulatory standards have rarely been matched in antiquity or modern times. Excelling in both founding and preserving, not to mention the Han, Tang, and Song, even Tang and Wu would yield to His illustrious achievements. His sacred virtue and divine功 (merits) are recorded in the Daily Records of the Great Ming (Da Ming rili) and the Record of Sacred Governance (Shengzheng ji). The Confucian officials of that time personally witnessed that flourishing era and reverently wrote prefaces to them: one said that His grand design was vast and far-reaching, and one said that the main principles were upheld and the details complete. The achievements of founding and preserving are fully set forth therein; can you point out and speak of His anxieties over the hardships from beginning to end?

His Majesty strenuously devotes Himself to sacred self-cultivation and keeps His eyes fixed upon the ancestral virtue. Recently, during the Classics Mat lectures and readings of the Ancestral Injunctions and Veritable Records, He first brought forward the compilation on the Hardships of Founding the Dynasty (Chuangye jiannan), repeatedly perusing and drawing out its meaning. The toils of ten years and a hundred battles, and the grand strategies of three twelve-year cycles of governance, are vividly present in the Sacred Mind; from dawn to night He plans for good order with ever greater diligence. Preserving the accomplishment and bringing about a flourishing age truly lies in the present day. Can you students also extol and display these achievements so as to reverently assist in even one part in ten thousand? If there is a single point worthy of adoption, it shall be reported upward to the Throne. Do not be cursory.

punctuated: 問：天人之際難言矣！以爲著，而轉移之機判於毫芒；以爲微，而休咎之徵捷於影響。《易》、《詩》、《書》、《春秋》深言之矣，可得明其旨歟？後世隂陽家占應禳除之議，儒者所不道；然陳規者往往稽之，使人主因事而戒，無亦不可廢歟？夫祥以祥應，灾以灾應，固宜；乃祥亦或爲灾，灾亦或爲祥，何說也？試以乘牒所紀論之：均之日五色也，五星聚也，甘露降、嘉禾生、黃河清、麒麟見，皆治象也，何以有治、有不治歟？均之亢陽也，流星也，狐升座、雉呴鼎、芝產殿、桑大拱，皆亂象也，何以有亂、有不亂歟？且灾非盛世所諱也。高皇帝時，稱彗見、稱客犯、稱太白熒惑者屢，而水旱螽螟之異亦時有之，乃鴻功駿業，千古莫及焉。所以爲昭格之本者，遵何道歟？我皇上敬
translation_en: Question: The interaction between Heaven and humankind is difficult to speak of! If one considers it manifest, the pivot of transformation is decided by the finest hair's breadth; if one considers it subtle, the signs of good and ill fortune respond more swiftly than shadow and echo. The Classic of Changes (Yi), the Classic of Poetry (Shi), the Classic of Documents (Shu), and the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) have spoken of this deeply; can their purport be elucidated? In later ages, the discussions of prognostication, correspondence, and apotropaic exorcism by the Yin-Yang school were things Confucian scholars did not speak of; yet those who present admonitions often examine them to cause the ruler to take warning from events—should they not also be kept from being discarded? Now, that auspiciousness responds with auspiciousness and disaster responds with disaster is certainly fitting; yet auspicious omens sometimes become disasters, and disasters sometimes become auspicious omens—what is the explanation for this? Let us discuss it through what is recorded in the historical annals: equally in all cases, a five-colored sun, a conjunction of the five planets, sweet dew descending, auspicious grain sprouting, the Yellow River running clear, and a unicorn (qilin) appearing are all signs of good governance—why then is there sometimes good governance and sometimes not? Equally in all cases, extreme drought, meteors, a fox ascending the throne, a pheasant crowing on a tripod, lingzhi mushrooms growing in the palace hall, and a mulberry tree growing to two-handed girth are all signs of disorder—why then is there sometimes disorder and sometimes not? Moreover, disasters are not something that a flourishing age shuns mentioning. In the time of the Exalted Emperor (Gao Huangdi, i.e., Emperor Taizu), there were repeated reports of comets appearing, of guest stars trespassing, and of Venus (Taibai) and Mars (Yinghuo), while anomalies of floods, droughts, locusts, and grain-borers also occurred from time to time; yet his vast achievements and magnificent enterprise have never been matched throughout antiquity. 天之誠，上繩祖武。往者星變而董百官，河决而詔眾議，賑荒則發帑蠲租，憂旱則齋居露禱，宜時和嵗豐，天庥滋至矣。而何以西北攙槍，邊陲流火，都城大癘，暵霪相仍？將數有適然歟？抑天心仁愛無窮歟？夫修德弭災，畏天時保，固聖衷所皇皇，而大小臣工不敢一息寧者也。有可指言得失，為今日交儆之助者，亟願聞之。

問：經以道法勝，史以事辭勝，厥惟舊矣。乃史之體亦有二焉：左氏編年，其稱也品藻，將無猶有道法者存歟？子長傳紀，其稱也實錄，得無儉于事辭之謂歟？後世作史者無慮數十百家，若荀悅、袁宏、習鑿齒、范祖禹，皆胤左氏而史者也，其品藻得失亦有可考歟？若班固、范曄、李延壽、歐陽脩，皆憲子長而史者也，其實錄
translation_en:
… Heaven specifically follows in the footsteps of His Ancestors. In the past, when celestial anomalies appeared, He admonished the hundred officials; when the Yellow River breached its banks, He issued an edict for broad deliberation; to relieve famine, He disbursed treasury funds and remitted taxes; worried by drought, He fasted in seclusion and prayed in the open air. Thus, the seasons ought to have been harmonious, the harvests abundant, and Heaven's blessings arriving in ever greater measure. Why, then, has a comet appeared in the northwest, meteors streamed across the frontier borders, a great epidemic struck the capital, and drought and excessive rain followed one upon another? Is this merely a coincidence of fate, or is it that Heaven's benevolent love is boundless? Cultivating virtue to avert disaster, standing in awe of Heaven so as constantly to preserve its favor—this is indeed what fills the Sagely Mind with anxious concern, and what prevents all officials, great and small, from resting for even a single breath. If you can point out the successes and failures so as to aid in our mutual admonition today, I earnestly wish to hear it.

Question: That the Classics excel in moral principles and models, whereas histories excel in events and literary expression, is a distinction of long standing. Yet historical writing itself has two main forms. Zuo Qiuming's (左氏) annalistic style is praised for its critical evaluation (pinzao)—does this not mean that moral principles and models are still preserved within it? Sima Qian's (Zizhang 子長) biographical-annalistic style is praised as a "veritable record" (shilu)—does this not mean that it is restricted merely to events and literary expression? In later generations, those who wrote histories numbered roughly dozens or hundreds of schools. Writers such as Xun Yue (荀悅), Yuan Hong (袁宏), Xi Zaochi (習鑿齒), and Fan Zuyu (范祖禹) all inherited Zuo Qiuming's tradition in writing history; can the merits and defects of their critical evaluations also be examined? Writers such as Ban Gu (班固), Fan Ye (范曄), Li Yanshou (李延壽), and Ouyang Xiu (歐陽脩) all modeled themselves on Sima Qian in writing history; as for the … of their veritable records…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
醇疵亦有可數歟遡惟宣聖文因魯史
義存王略作春秋以垂勸戒固史中之
經也萬世之言史者宜不能越矣寥寥
數千載後有宋朱仲晦氏作乃因溫公
之通鑑標綱目以爲書以上接麟經而
下苞羣史不知其於道法事辭品藻實
錄爲何如亦有合於孔氏之指否歟諸
士子究心史學宜必有所折衷矣請詳
言之用觀良史于他日
===
問士君子之在天地間不學入何事矣學
也者吾所𢘆成其身自盡其分之事也
而古今之人才高下世道升降繫之惡
可以不講也顧今世之學者不明于其
術而徒以嘵嘵取天下之誚吾甚惑之
孔子曰學之不講是吾憂也然則孔子
非歟論學莫如唐虞人才世道稱極盛
矣無非學也而未甞言學下此若終始
典學之告君學古入官之訓士蓋始諄

經也萬世之言史者宜不能越矣寥寥

士子究心史學宜必有所折衷矣請詳
言之用觀良史于他日
===
問士君子之在天地間不學又何事矣學
也者吾所曾成其身自盡其分之事也
而古今之人才高下世道升降繫之焉
可以不講也顧今世之學者不明于其
術而徒以曉曉取天下之誚吾甚惑之
孔子曰學之不講是吾憂也然則孔子
非歟論學莫如唐虞人才世道稱極盛
矣無非學也而未嘗言學下此若終始
典學之告君學古入官之訓士蓋鯑譯
punctuated:
醇疵亦有可數歟？遡惟宣聖，文因魯史，義存王略，作《春秋》以垂勸戒，固史中之經也，萬世之言史者宜不能越矣。寥寥數千載後，有宋朱仲晦氏作，乃因溫公之《通鑑》，標綱目以爲書，以上接《麟經》而下苞羣史。不知其於道法、事辭、品藻、實錄爲何如？亦有合於孔氏之指否歟？諸士子究心史學，宜必有所折衷矣。請詳言之，用觀良史于他日。
問：士君子之在天地間，不學入何事矣？學也者，吾所𢘆成其身、自盡其分之事也，而古今之人才高下、世道升降繫之，惡可以不講也？顧今世之學者，不明于其術，而徒以嘵嘵取天下之誚，吾甚惑之。孔子曰：「學之不講，是吾憂也。」然則孔子非歟？論學莫如唐虞，人才、世道稱極盛矣，無非學也，而未甞言學。下此，若「終始典學」之告君，「學古入官」之訓士，蓋始諄
translation_en:
… can the purity and flaws [of their "veritable records"] also be enumerated? Tracing back to the Sage of Exalted Culture [Confucius], he based his text on the annals of Lu and preserved in its meaning the grand design of the true kings, composing the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) to hand down encouragement and admonition. Truly it is a Classic among histories, which those who speak of history for ten thousand generations ought not to be able to surpass. After a sparse expanse of several thousand years, Master Zhu Zhonghui [Zhu Xi 朱熹] of the Song arose; building upon the Comprehensive Mirror (Tongjian) of Duke Wen [Sima Guang 司馬光], he set forth "outlines" (gang) and "details" (mu) to make a book [the Tongjian gangmu], connecting above with the Classic of the Unicorn [the Spring and Autumn Annals] and encompassing all the histories below. How does it stand with respect to moral principles and models, events and diction, critical appraisal, and veritable recording? Does it also accord with the intent of Master Kong [Confucius], or not? You gentlemen have devoted your minds to the study of history and surely have reached a balanced judgment. Please speak of this in detail, so that we may behold fine historians in a future day.

Question: Standing between heaven and earth, if a scholar-gentleman does not engage in learning, what business does he have [reading 入 as 人/又]? Learning is the business whereby we constantly [reading 𢘆 as 以自 or 恒] perfect our own persons and fulfill our own allotted duties; yet the superiority or inferiority of talent and the rise or decline of the moral order of the world in ancient and modern times are bound up with it—how could it not be discussed and expounded? Yet scholars of the present age are unclear about its method, and merely by their noisy wrangling draw the ridicule of the world; I am deeply puzzled by this. Confucius said: "That learning is not discussed and practiced is my worry." Was Confucius then wrong? In speaking of learning, no era surpasses Tang [Yao] and Yu [Shun], when human talent and the way of the world were acclaimed as at their utmost flourishing; nothing then was not learning, and yet they never spoke of "learning." Coming down from this, with counsels to the ruler such as "from beginning to end constantly cleave to learning" [in the Book of Documents] and instructions to officials such as "study antiquity in order to enter office," people first began earnestly…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
諄焉不知三代所學者何事亦嘗講之
口耳否歟其所以享國長久與後世迥
異者亦繋諸此否歟
今天下人才非不彬彬而學之術槩乎未之
講也又且以為諱然則亦遂因循于晩
近世之陋而隆古之盛治將使
聖朝終不可復睹歟是必有司之者矣故吾今
亦不暇鉤深策隱重蠱諸士而相願以
士君子學術與共商之
===
問國有大務雖棊隆之世不可斯須忘者
邊備是也昔之人嘗言夷狄強弱自有
時顧中國內治如何中國治夷狄雖強
無深害而弱則有成功中國不治夷狄
雖弱不為福而強則為深害故漢自高
文以來雖有白登之圍甘泉之警而無
損於治宣元以還郅支呼韓之朝相望
而無益玆已事也然謂之無益可已而
宋儒乃論漢之衰自宣帝始無乃言之

口耳否歟其所以享國長久與後世迥
異者亦繫諸此否歟

亦不暇鉤深策隱重蠱諸士而相願以
士君子學術與共商之
===
問國有大務雖綦隆之世不可斯須忘者
邊備是也昔之人嘗言夷狄强弱自有
時顧中國內治如何中國治夷狄雖强
無深害而弱則有成功中國不治夷狄
雖弱不爲福而强則爲深害故漢用高
文以來雖有白登之圍甘泉之警而無
損於治宣元以還郅支呼韓之朝相望
而無益茲已事也然謂之無益可已而
宋儒乃論漢之衰自宣帝始無乃言之
punctuated:
諄焉。不知三代所學者何事，亦嘗講之口耳否歟？其所以享國長久，與後世迥異者，亦繋諸此否歟？今天下人才非不彬彬，而學之術槩乎未之講也，又且以為諱。然則亦遂因循于晩近世之陋，而隆古之盛治，將使聖朝終不可復睹歟？是必有司之者矣。故吾今亦不暇鉤深策隱，重蠱諸士，而相願以士君子學術與共商之。

問：國有大務，雖棊隆之世不可斯須忘者，邊備是也。昔之人嘗言，夷狄強弱自有時，顧中國內治如何。中國治，夷狄雖強無深害，而弱則有成功；中國不治，夷狄雖弱不為福，而強則為深害。故漢自高、文以來，雖有白登之圍、甘泉之警，而無損於治；宣、元以還，郅支、呼韓之朝相望，而無益。玆已事也。然謂之無益可已，而宋儒乃論漢之衰自宣帝始，無乃言之
translation_en:
…earnestly repeated. We do not know what it was that was studied during the Three Dynasties, or whether they too merely discussed it by mouth and ear? Was the reason they enjoyed long-lasting rule, so utterly different from later ages, also tied to this or not? Today, men of talent in the empire are not lacking in refinement, yet the art of learning is generally left undiscussed, and is even treated as a taboo. If so, shall we simply follow the vulgar ways of recent ages, so that the flourishing governance of high antiquity will never again be witnessed by our Sacred Dynasty? Surely there must be those who bear responsibility for this. Therefore, I now have no leisure to probe into abstruse and hidden matters to further perplex you gentlemen, and instead wish to deliberate together with you on the learning and art of the scholar-gentleman.

Question: The state has a great affair which, even in an era of supreme prosperity [?], cannot be forgotten for a single moment: this is frontier defense. People of the past once said that the strength or weakness of the barbarians has its own times, and what matters is the state of China's internal governance. When China is well governed, even if the barbarians are strong they cause no deep harm, and if they are weak, success is achieved; when China is not well governed, even if the barbarians are weak it is no blessing, and if they are strong they become a deep harm. Thus in the Han, from the time of Emperors Gaozu and Wen onward, although there was the siege at Baideng and the alarm at Ganquan, these did no damage to good governance; from the reigns of Emperors Xuan and Yuan onward, the court visits of Zhizhi and Huhanye followed one after another in view, yet were of no benefit. These are bygone affairs. Yet while it is permissible to call them of no benefit, Song-dynasty Confucians argued that the decline of the Han began with Emperor Xuan—is that not speaking…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
過歟或又盛稱宣帝中興之功在兼夷
狄其論懸絕如此孰爲當歟當時內治
得失之繇可指而言歟虜入我
國家其創鉅甚矣然白登甘泉之事間嘗有
之而郅支呼韓之來方在
今日豈非增光
祖宗之盛千載一時哉毋謂虜易與我之所以
藩固邊圉計安黎庶而永保順治威嚴
之績者不可不鑒宣元之際也雖
===
廟堂石畫自在而諸生胡寧不念此其試言之
各效其憂治危明之志焉

之而郅支呼韓之來方在

藩固邊圉計安黎庶而永保順治威嚴
之績者不可不鑒宣元之際也雖
===
廟堂石畫自在而諸生胡寧不念此其試言之
各效其憂治危明之志焉
punctuated: 過歟？或又盛稱宣帝中興之功在兼夷狄，其論懸絕如此，孰爲當歟？當時內治得失之繇，可指而言歟？虜入我國家，其創鉅甚矣。然白登、甘泉之事，間嘗有之，而郅支、呼韓之來，方在今日，豈非增光祖宗之盛，千載一時哉！毋謂虜易與，我之所以藩固邊圉、計安黎庶，而永保順治威嚴之績者，不可不鑒宣、元之際也。雖廟堂石畫自在，而諸生胡寧不念此？其試言之，各效其憂治危明之志焉。
translation_en:
…excessive? Others, conversely, lavishly praise Emperor Xuan's achievement of dynastic restoration as lying in his incorporation of the foreign tribes. With these arguments so utterly at odds, which one is right? Can the reasons for the successes and failures of internal governance at that time be pointed out and discussed?

The northern nomads' incursions into our State have inflicted grievous wounds indeed. Yet while incidents like those at Baideng and Ganquan have occurred from time to time, the submission of leaders like Zhizhi and Huhanye is happening right now in our own day—is this not an unprecedented moment in a thousand years that adds luster to the flourishing achievements of our Ancestors! Still, do not say that the northern nomads are easy to deal with. In the ways by which we fortify our frontier defenses, plan for the security of the common people, and forever preserve the achievements of compliant order and awe-inspiring dignity, we cannot fail to take the reigns of Emperors Xuan and Yuan as our mirror. Although the rock-solid counsels of the imperial court are already in place, how could you students not give thought to this? Try to set forth your views, each of you demonstrating your resolve to worry in times of order and be vigilant in an age of enlightenment.

text:

四書

高洪謨
同考試官教諭丘批典實不浮發意有體

The Sage discusses the supremacy of the virtue of the Mean, and deeply laments over the common people. Now, virtue takes the Mean as its supreme perfection, and the common people are all capable of it; yet they have lacked it for a long time—why is this? This is why the Master lamented. title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
人之所受而措之適協於時乃三極之定理其
知常知也而性命精微之具於是乎存實知之
至焉易知之知聖人不能易矣其行常行也而
聖神功化之極於是焉在實行之至焉簡能之
能作者無以加矣顧性雖同命於天不能不待
教而明今之世智者愚者皆昧焉而孰能有明
也道雖同率於性不能不待教而行今之世賢
者不肖者胥失焉而孰能有行也道不可一毫
有加而以意加之旣日荒於隱怪而不返道不
===
可一毫有損而以意損之又日流於卑下而不
知民之鮮能豈一朝一夕之故哉弊也久矣有
世教之責者不可諉也抑中庸之德學者爲難
而何以槩責之民哉夫堯舜之民默順帝則三
代之民直道而行卽中庸也天下之患莫大於
舍常事而飾詭業而愚柔者不與焉飾愚以爲
智飾不肖以爲賢常在於學者而其究不著只
民噫曷不爲中庸之易而至于敝天下也學者
其尚戒哉

其尚戒哉
punctuated: 人之所受，而措之適協於時，乃三極之定理。其知，常知也；而性命精微之具於是乎存，實知之至焉，易知之知，聖人不能易矣。其行，常行也；而聖神功化之極於是焉在，實行之至焉，簡能之能，作者無以加矣。顧性雖同命於天，不能不待教而明，今之世智者、愚者皆昧焉，而孰能有明也？道雖同率於性，不能不待教而行，今之世賢者、不肖者胥失焉，而孰能有行也？道不可一毫有加，而以意加之，旣日荒於隱怪而不返；道不可一毫有損，而以意損之，又日流於卑下而不知。民之鮮能，豈一朝一夕之故哉？弊也久矣，有世教之責者不可諉也。抑中庸之德，學者爲難，而何以槩責之民哉？夫堯、舜之民，默順帝則；三代之民，直道而行，卽中庸也。天下之患，莫大於舍常事而飾詭業，而愚柔者不與焉。飾愚以爲智，飾不肖以爲賢，常在於學者，而其究不著只民。噫！曷不爲中庸之易，而至于敝天下也？學者其尚戒哉！
translation_en:
…what people receive at birth, and when put into practice it accords precisely with the times, being the constant principle of the Three Ultimates. Its knowledge is ordinary knowledge, yet within it resides the subtle totality of human nature and Heaven's mandate; it is truly the perfection of knowledge—the knowledge of what is easy to know, which even a sage cannot alter. Its practice is ordinary practice, yet within it lies the ultimate transformative achievement of sagely and spiritual power; it is truly the perfection of practice—the capability of what is simple to do, to which even the creative sages could add nothing.

Yet although human nature is equally conferred by Heaven, it cannot become clear without awaiting instruction; in the present age both the wise and the foolish are alike in the dark about it, so who is able to clarify it? Although the Way equally follows from human nature, it cannot be put into practice without awaiting instruction; in the present age both the worthy and the unworthy alike lose sight of it, so who is able to practice it? Not a hair's breadth may be added to the Way, yet people add to it out of private whim, growing daily more lost in obscurity and怪eccentricity without turning back; not a hair's breadth may be subtracted from the Way, yet people subtract from it out of private whim, sinking daily further into baseness without realizing it. That the common people are rarely able to practice it—how could this be the result of a single morning or evening? The decay has lasted for a long time, and those who bear responsibility for the moral instruction of the world cannot shirk it.

Moreover, if the virtue of the Constant Mean is difficult even for scholars, how can one sweepingly demand it of the common people? The people of Yao and Shun silently complied with the Sovereign's norm, and the people of the Three Dynasties walked the straight Way—that was itself the Constant Mean. The greatest misfortune in the world is to abandon ordinary duties and deck out deceptive enterprises, and in this the foolish and weak have no part. Decking out folly as wisdom and unworthiness as worthiness is constantly found among scholars, until in the end its harm extends even to the common people [?]. Alas! Why do they not practice the ease of the Constant Mean, instead of bringing ruin upon the world? Let scholars take warning indeed!

Associate Examiner, Instructor Li, comments: "He develops the theme of employing the worthy with a pure heart; the thought is incisive and thorough, and the phrasing is even more ancient and elegant. It is the finest of the essays on the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong)."

Only when one employs the worthy with a pure heart does the way of encouraging the worthy reside therein. Indeed, when a ruler's heart is divided, the worthy will not be of service to him. Is it not for this reason that a pure heart is the way to encourage the worthy? When the Master spoke to Duke Ai (Ai Gong 哀公), it was as if he said: Only when there are both the right ruler and the right ministers can the governance of the former kings be raised up; thus, apart from cultivating one's own person, nothing is more urgent than honoring the worthy. Yet how are the worthy to be encouraged? In entrusting responsibilities to the worthy, a ruler relies solely upon this heart of his. If he mixes slanderers into it, his heart becomes suspicious; if he mixes a fondness for sensual beauty into it, his heart becomes dissipated; if he mixes a fondness for material goods into it, his heart becomes sullied. That is not entrusting responsibilities to the worthy with purity. He must banish slanderers and flatterers, not allowing them to delude his ears; dismiss alluring beauties, not allowing them to dazzle his eyes; and renounce goods and wealth, not allowing them to ruin his determination. 私，意念所注，惟有德之是親；歡然兩相遇合，而精神所孚，惟輔德之是急。如此，可謂眞貴德矣，非所以勸賢乎？吾知憸夫宵人之言不入，則賢士大夫之心畢歸；聲色貨利之好旣徹，則道術博聞之士自集。上不疑，下不忌，何所憚而不竭股肱之力？君曰「都」，臣曰「俞」，何所隔而不成上下之交？賢之勸也，宜矣。不然，賢者亦欲自完也、自好也、自寶也，而肯輕試乎哉？吁！此九經之要務也。然賢者，人主之所尊也；彼三者，人主之所狎也。尊者易疎，狎者易溺，人情乎！而况賢者常制其所欲，彼以三說進者，又常媒孽其間，而賢者危矣。故惟聖王而後能無欲，無欲而後能純心用賢，此又以身取人者所當念也。

… bias, and what one's thoughts and intentions are fixed upon is solely to draw close to the virtuous; when both meet in joyful harmony, and what their spirits trust in is solely the urgent task of assisting virtue—like this, one can truly be said to prize virtue! Is this not the way to encourage the worthy? I know that when the words of sycophants and petty men do not enter, the hearts of worthy scholars and great officers will all turn in allegiance; once the fondness for music, women, wealth, and profit is removed, scholars of the Way and of broad learning will naturally gather. When the ruler above does not suspect and those below do not resent, what would they fear that would keep them from exhausting the strength of their limbs in service? When the ruler says, "Oh!" and the minister says, "Yes!", what barrier could prevent the consummation of fellowship between above and below? That the worthy are encouraged is only fitting! Otherwise, the worthy also wish to preserve themselves, to cherish their own integrity, and to treasure themselves—would they be willing to lightly put themselves to the test? Alas! This is an essential task among the Nine Standard Rules of governance. Yet the worthy are those whom the ruler reveres, whereas those other three are what the ruler treats with familiar intimacy. Those whom one reveres are easily kept at a distance, while what one treats with familiarity is easy to drown in—such is human nature! How much more so when the worthy constantly restrain the ruler's desires, while those who advance by means of those three enticements constantly intrigue and foment trouble between them, placing the worthy in peril! Therefore, only a sage king can be free of desires, and only by being free of desires can he employ the worthy with a pure heart. This, too, is what one who attracts men through his own person ought to bear in mind.

The governance of the Two Emperors was a matter of laboring with their minds for All under Heaven. For governance is rooted in the mind; when Yao and Shun labored for All under Heaven with their minds, was not the application of their minds great indeed? By this Mencius refuted Xu Xing. Moreover, governance has its fundamental substance, for which one must surely first recognize what is great; and governance has its essential pivot, which lies solely in making good use of one's mind. Reasoning from the terms in which Confucius praised Yao and Shun, one knows the error of the doctrine of ruler and subject plowing side by side. For Yao's realm was governed by Yao—it was not that he had nothing whatever to attend to; within his accomplished and thoughtful character there must have been a spirit operating in solitary mastery. Shun's realm was governed by Shun—he did not busy himself with petty trifles; within his profound intelligence there must have been considerations of the greatest magnitude. When the primordial chaos had just been opened up, what limit was there to the responsibilities that the mind of Heaven laid upon the ruler above? Yao and Shun took the mind of Heaven as their own mind and sought to carry it forward—how could they remain indifferent above? When administrative order and moral instruction had not yet been spread abroad, what end was there to the hopes that the minds of the people looked up to from below? Yao and Shun took the minds of the people as their own mind and sought to comfort them—how could they remain unconcerned below? "Patterning himself on Heaven, so vast that the people could find no name for it"—this speaks only of how his imperial virtue was forgotten by the people. translation_en:
… bringing peace to all under heaven, they pondered from dawn till night without ever allowing themselves to relax. Otherwise, what sort of towering achievement was that, and how could it have been accomplished with an unconcerned mind? To sum it up [?], great men make laboring with their minds their business, and the benevolent find worthy men for the empire. Yao's mind was devoted to finding Shun, and Shun's mind was devoted to finding Yu and Gao Yao; that ten thousand generations acclaim them as great sovereigns is entirely because of this. How could it be a matter of plowing side by side with the people! Extreme indeed was the fallacy of Xu Xing! Yet if we discuss who best understood the minds of Yao and Shun, none surpassed Mencius, because he spoke of their deep anxiety and the difficulty of finding the right men. Still, if we take those words literally, would it mean that before finding such men they were anxious, and once having found them they immediately felt relieved and had no further need to exercise their minds? In essence, in "being Refined and Single-minded, and holding fast the Mean," the cautious diligence of Yao and Shun never ceased, and their benevolence covered all under heaven—so that even to say their minds survive to this very day is permissible. Those who model themselves on Yao and Shun ought to make Yao and Shun's minds their own.

者夫人心易離亦易玩也孚以固之威以厲之
有其常保哉且人主處有大之時盛衰倚伏之
機在焉可使精神一日不流於人心哉故周公
係五之辭曰厥孚交如夫人主何以貴孚也天
下之志孰無忠君親上之誠而惟信足以發之

下有不二心之臣上惠心斯下有惠我德之眾
蓋本吾之情以一萬物之情而上下之精神始
會聚而不可解同心一統之義如是耳不然人
心幾何其不離耶又曰威如之吉夫人主何以
貴威也天下之釁常萌於治平無事之時而惟

眾必操吾之重以衡天下之輕而上下之精神

In explaining the line of Great Possession (Dayou), the Commentary on the Images (Xiangzhuan) shows that by which men's minds are bound fast, and that by which men's minds are spurred to awe. Now, men's minds easily become alienated, and easily grow lax as well. By sincerity one binds them fast, and by majesty one spurs them to awe—thus may great possession be forever preserved! Moreover, when a ruler occupies a time of great possession, the pivot upon which flourishing and decline mutually depend lies therein; how could he allow his vital spirit not to flow through the minds of men for even a single day?

Therefore the Duke of Zhou attached the words to the Fifth line, saying: "His sincerity is reciprocated." Why does a ruler prize sincerity? Among the aspirations of all under Heaven, who lacks the genuine devotion to be loyal to the sovereign and attached to superiors? Yet only trustworthiness is sufficient to bring it forth. The Fifth line empties himself to associate with those below; he extends trustworthiness and others trust him. For this reason, when the ruler above is single-minded [?], below there will be ministers of undivided heart; when the ruler above has a benevolent heart, below there will be a multitude that conforms to his virtue. Indeed, one bases oneself on one's own sentiments in order to unify the sentiments of the myriad things, and only then does the vital spirit of above and below converge and become inseparable. Such is the meaning of shared hearts and unified rule. Otherwise, how long would it be before men's minds become alienated?

It also says: "The good fortune of his majesty." Why does a ruler prize majesty? Rifts in the realm constantly sprout in times of peaceful order and freedom from trouble, and only firmness is sufficient to keep them in check. If one relies exclusively on gentleness, one grows lax oneself and others will treat one lightly. For this reason, when overall control is slack, the abuse of neglecting official duties proliferates; when perfunctory routine continues for long, the people who violate the law become numerous. One must wield one's own weight to counterbalance the lightness of the world, so that the vital spirit of above and below…

… [stays] in vigilant awe and dares not grow lax; such is the authority that whets the age and sharpens the dull. Otherwise, how long would it take before people's hearts grew trifling? Ah! Is it not through these three things that one can illuminate and rally the sentiments of all, govern the six directions of the universe, and preserve and ever enlarge one's heritage across generations? Yet in the well-governed ages of antiquity, when all shared one virtue and one mind and the realm attained supreme order, the efficacy of sincerity and trustworthiness could already be seen—what need was there for majesty? Indeed, a ruler's virtue prizes firmness, and an age of Great Possession (Dayou) especially cannot be governed by the way of softness. Wind, thunder, and scorching sun cannot be dispensed with even by Heaven—how much less in governing the realm! Even so, in "repressing evil and exalting the good," there is no majesty greater than this; how could binding firewood and twisting ropes [i.e., harsh, petty punishments] be true majesty? This, too, is what one who occupies an age of abundance ought to know.

未及聞而神之聽之甚於民聽焉善惡之徵捷
若響應也居室之行民未及見而神之視之甚
於民視焉應違之機疾若景從也夫觀所感於
人心則榮辱相生之端已爲可畏觀所感於天
===

而民可知矣君子所以長享天下之榮者以是
哉夫人主居於民上徒曰惟其言行而莫予違
也則何難者而不知啓口舉足天與人交察焉

punctuated: 觀言行通乎造化，而君子當謹焉。夫天地大矣，君子之言行足以動之，而何可以弗謹哉？且夫樞機之發，榮辱係焉，君子之所以動民者，則已神矣。豈惟民哉？天地之於人也，常監於不言不動之中，而顯於有言有動之際。故居室之言，民未及聞，而神之聽之，甚於民聽焉，善惡之徵，捷若響應也；居室之行，民未及見，而神之視之，甚於民視焉，應違之機，疾若景從也。夫觀所感於人心，則榮辱相生之端已爲可畏；觀所感於天地，則天人相與之際尤爲甚嚴。故言可易也，而天地之聽聞在焉，惡得而易之？蓋必信於不言，又擬於將言，苟不可使聞于天地，不以出諸口可也。行可忽也，而天地之監觀在焉，惡得而忽諸？蓋必敬於不動，又議於將動，苟不可使見於天也，不以措諸身可也。言行交愼，則天地如之，而民可知矣，君子所以長享天下之榮者，以是哉！夫人主居於民上，徒曰惟其言行而莫予違也，則何難者？而不知啓口舉足，天與人交察焉，
translation_en: Observing how words and deeds communicate with the creative transformations of nature, the noble man must be cautious about them. Now, vast indeed are Heaven and Earth! If the words and deeds of the noble man are sufficient to move them, how could he fail to be cautious? Moreover, upon the triggering of this pivot and spring, glory and disgrace depend; the means by which the noble man moves the people is already wondrous. Yet is it only the people? In their relation to humanity, Heaven and Earth constantly inspect us while we have not yet spoken or acted, and manifest their response at the moment we speak and act. Therefore, before the words spoken in one's chamber have even been heard by the people, the spirits hear them more acutely than the people do; the signs of good and evil respond as swiftly as an echo. Before the deeds done in one's chamber have even been seen by the people, the spirits see them more acutely than the people do; the mechanism of accord and defiance follows as rapidly as a shadow. Now, if we observe how they affect the minds of the people, the beginnings from which glory and disgrace mutually arise are already awe-inspiring; if we observe how they affect Heaven and Earth, the interaction between Heaven and humanity is all the more strictly rigorous. Therefore, one might think words can be treated lightly, yet the hearing of Heaven and Earth is present—how could one treat them lightly? Indeed, one must be truthful before speaking, and deliberate when about to speak; if something cannot be allowed to be heard by Heaven and Earth, one should simply not let it issue from one's mouth. One might think deeds can be neglected, yet the watchful observation of Heaven and Earth is present—how could one neglect them? Indeed, one must be reverent before acting, and consider when about to act; if something cannot be allowed to be seen by Heaven [and Earth], one should simply not put it into practice in one's person. When words and deeds are both attended to with caution, Heaven and Earth will respond in kind, and the response of the people can be known as well. Is it not by this means that the noble man long enjoys the glory of the world! Now, when a ruler of men dwells above the people, if he merely says that in his words and deeds none shall oppose him, what difficulty would there be? Yet he fails to realize that whenever he opens his mouth or lifts his foot, Heaven and humanity both examine him; …

聖臣啓帝念保治之謨，而因詳其道焉。夫致治難，保治尤難也。養道成而保之于終，非帝所當念者哉？昔禹歎而陳于帝曰：天下之治，始乎盛，
translation_en:
…its subtle stirrings are most minute, yet its principle is most manifest; it is greatly to be feared. Master Dong [Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒], extrapolating from the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) to speak of Heaven and Man, also took words and deeds as the foundation, saying: "He who exhausts the small achieves the great; he who is cautious of the minute becomes manifest." Truly, he understood the purport of the Book of Changes (Yi)!

Book of Documents (Shu)

"Yu said: 'Oh! May the Sovereign bear this in mind! Virtue is seen in good government, and government is tested by the nourishing of the people. Water, fire, metal, wood, earth, and grain must be regulated; the rectification of virtue, the convenience of life's utilities, and the securing of abundant livelihood must be harmonized. When these nine achievements are all orderly, all nine orders may be celebrated in song. Admonish them with felicities, correct them with majesty, and encourage them with the nine songs, so that success may never be ruined.'"

Shen Zan 沈瓚

Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Lu comments: The Yu minister's [Yu's] heart of love for his ruler placed great weight on preserving good governance, and this essay alone is able to bring that out. Moreover, its diction and reasoning are refined and pure, and its train of thought is deep and closely knit; it can serve as a model.
Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Zhao comments: Finely structured in thought and pure in its literary expression, it vividly brings out the ancient loyal minister's intention of preserving good governance; this writer too is one who harbors a heart of loyalty and affection.
Examiner and Expositor-in-waiting Han comments: A penetrating and thorough argument.
Examiner and Left Admonisher Zhu comments: Unadulterated, with refined elegance.

The sagely minister inspires the Sovereign to bear in mind the counsels for preserving good governance, and thereupon elaborates its way in detail. Now, to bring about good governance is difficult, and to preserve good governance is even more difficult. When the way of nourishing the people has been accomplished, to preserve it to the end—is this not what the Sovereign ought to bear in mind? Of old, Yu sighed and set forth before the Sovereign, saying: The governance of all under Heaven begins in flourishing…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
常卒乎衰何也始未嘗不儆戒而後稍怠荒也
益欲儆戒無虞帝其念哉念之若何蓋君非徒
德也貴乎有以善其政政非徒善也在乎有以
養其民今禹有裁成天地之德政而水火金木
土穀六者無不修有輔相民物之德政而正德
利用厚生三者無不和惟府事之修和也而九
功悉見其順叙惟九功之旣叙也而九歌自發
爲治徵世至此可謂無虞矣然豈可以遽忘儆
戒乎哉蓋勤始怠終之民必待鼓舞於勸相而
===
久安長治之業要在流通其精神以休命而戒
之作其勤也以威命而董之懲其怠也而猶未
也慮其勤之難繼也而九歌勸焉卽其發於咏
歌者以動其思而人心益勵矣成者豈復壞乎
慮其怠之易乘也而勸以歌焉卽其播于心聲
者以動其天而美業益固矣治者不常治乎蓋
必如是則德政日新民養恒裕是儆戒無虞之
道也帝其念之甞繹是而知聲音之道與政通
也在治忽以五言訓頑讒以納言帝亦有感於

punctuated: 常卒乎衰，何也？始未嘗不儆戒，而後稍怠荒也。益欲「儆戒無虞」，帝其念哉！念之若何？蓋君非徒德也，貴乎有以善其政；政非徒善也，在乎有以養其民。今禹有裁成天地之德政，而水、火、金、木、土、穀六者無不修；有輔相民物之德政，而正德、利用、厚生三者無不和。惟府事之修和也，而九功悉見其順叙；惟九功之旣叙也，而九歌自發爲治徵。世至此，可謂無虞矣。然豈可以遽忘儆戒乎哉？蓋勤始怠終之民，必待鼓舞於勸相；而久安長治之業，要在流通其精神。以休命而戒之，作其勤也；以威命而董之，懲其怠也。而猶未也。慮其勤之難繼也，而九歌勸焉，卽其發於咏歌者以動其思，而人心益勵矣，成者豈復壞乎？慮其怠之易乘也，而勸以歌焉，卽其播于心聲者以動其天，而美業益固矣，治者不常治乎？蓋必如是，則德政日新，民養恒裕，是「儆戒無虞」之道也，帝其念之！甞繹是而知聲音之道與政通也。在治忽以五言，訓頑讒以納言，帝亦有感於…
translation_en: …commonly ends in decline—why is that? Because in the beginning one never fails to be vigilant and cautious, yet later grows somewhat indolent and neglectful. Boyi wished for "vigilance and caution when there is no cause for anxiety"—may the Emperor bear this in mind! How should he bear it in mind? Indeed, a ruler does not rely on virtue alone; what is prized is having the means to perfect his governance. Governance does not rely on goodness alone; it lies in having the means to nourish his people. Now I, Yu, possess the virtuous governance that regulates and completes heaven and earth, so that the six treasuries of water, fire, metal, wood, earth, and grain are all well-managed; and I possess the virtuous governance that assists and supports the people and things, so that the three affairs of rectifying virtue, improving the tools of life, and enriching livelihoods are all harmonized. Because the six treasuries and three affairs are well-managed and harmonized, the nine achievements all manifest their proper order; and once the nine achievements are in order, the nine songs naturally arise as tokens of good governance. When the world reaches this point, it may truly be called free of cause for anxiety. Yet how could one suddenly forget vigilance and caution? For a populace that is diligent at the start and indolent at the end must depend on being roused through encouragement and mutual aid, while an enterprise of lasting peace and enduring order hinges upon keeping its vital spirit circulating. By warning them with gracious commands, one stirs up their diligence; by supervising them with stern commands, one punishes their indolence. Yet even this is not enough. Worrying that their diligence is hard to sustain, one encourages them with the nine songs—using what is expressed in chanting and singing to move their thoughts, so that people's minds are ever more inspired; how then could what has been accomplished be ruined again? Worrying that indolence easily creeps in, one encourages them through song—using what is broadcast as the voice of the heart to move their innate nature, so that the fine enterprise grows ever firmer; will what is well-governed not remain forever well-governed? Only when it is necessarily like this will virtuous governance be daily renewed and the nourishment of the people remain constantly abundant. This is the Way of "vigilance and caution when there is no cause for anxiety"—may the Emperor bear it in mind! I have reflected upon this and know that the Way of sounds and music communicates with governance. Examining order and neglect through the five notes and speeches, and instructing the obstinate and slanderous by receiving their words—was the Emperor Shun not also moved by…

聖王論化民，期於和之而已。蓋寬而有以濟之，則和矣，然豈可以欲速焉哉？成王命君陳和中，若曰：政必因時而立，化以持久而成。今非謹毖之時，威削所不用矣。公欲善治，其寬之乎！含弘光大，擴天地之量而不私；豈第慈祥，推父母之…
translation_en:
… the counsels of the Nine Songs, and therefore specially charged Yu with this task? From the decline of the Zhou dynasty onward, the feudal lords no longer presented odes as tribute, the Son of Heaven no longer collected airs of the states, and the world declined day by day. Alas! How far removed this is from the virtuous governance of the court of Yu [Shun]! What wonder is it that governance no longer matches that of antiquity?

"Be寬 [magnanimous] yet have regulations; be unhurried and thereby bring about harmony." [Book of Documents, "Jun Chen"]
Shen Yongmao 申用懋
Comment by Associate Examiner Assistant Instructor Lu 陸: King Cheng commanded Jun Chen 君陳 to harmonize the middle stage [of governance]. Most who write on this [? 皇之作者] treat magnanimity and harmony as parallel opposites; this essay alone says that magnanimity is used to achieve harmony, deeply grasping the original intent. None but a scholar superior in both learning and insight could reach this level; it should be selected for inclusion.
Comment by Associate Examiner Assistant Instructor Zhao 趙: Using regulated magnanimity to harmonize the people without precipitately demanding their transformation—this was King Cheng's original intent in harmonizing the middle stage. This essay expounds the meaning from within and furthermore expresses it in antique and elegant language. He is a scholar who has thoroughly mastered the classic; record it.
Comment by Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Han 韓: Vigorous, profound, and mature.
Comment by Examiner Left Admonisher Zhu 朱: Precise, fitting, classical, and weighty.

When the sage-king discussed transforming the people, he aimed solely at bringing them into harmony. Indeed, when one is magnanimous and yet has regulations to temper it, harmony is achieved; how, then, could one desire haste in this? When King Cheng commanded Jun Chen to harmonize the middle stage, it was as if he said: Governance must be established in accordance with the times, and transformation is achieved through sustained perseverance. Now is not a time for stern caution; severe and restrictive measures have no place. If you, Duke, wish to govern well, should you not be magnanimous? Be all-embracing, vast, and glorious, expanding a capacity like that of Heaven and Earth without partiality; be easygoing, joyous, kind, and benevolent, extending the grace of a father and mother…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
恩而無擇茹納之內規畫存焉俾驕矜者弗敢
肆足矣保愛之餘防閑密焉令怙侈者有所憚
足矣夫寬行於制之中而制不出於寬之外若
此者所以和之也然政有緩急不可凌其序而
雜施民有頑淳不可拂其性而加責教化未洽
假歲月以摩之優游浸漬自然淪浹於肌膚矣
習俗未消寬程限以率之馴擾調娛自然融液
於心志矣謂之曰和其庶幾乎至是則孝恭之
德已施於政而馨香之治可感乎神所以弘正
===
訓化殷民者至矣雖周公而在何以尚茲抑聞
之傳曰政寬則糾之以猛政猛則施之以寬寬
以濟猛猛以濟寬政是以和其說蓋出於此然
所謂猛者亦有制云爾豈遂束縛之馳驟之若
牛馬然乎即周公謹毖而云師保萬民民懷其
德似非專任威者三代聖人享國長久大都以
寬和民自火烈水弱之說行而申韓者流遂以
其學禍天下吁可鑒也
詩

於心志矣謂之曰和其庶幾乎至是則孝恭之
德已施於政而馨香之治可感乎神所以弘丕
===
訓化殷民者至矣雖周公而在何以尚茲抑聞
之傳曰政寬則糾之以猛政猛則施之以寬寬
以濟猛猛以濟寬政是以和其說蓋出於此然
所謂猛者亦有制云爾豈遂束縛之馳驟之若
牛馬然乎即周公謹毖而云師保萬民民懷其
德似非專任威者三代聖人享國長久大都以
寬和民自火烈水弱之說行而申韓者流遂以
其學禍天下吁可鑒也
詩
punctuated:
恩而無擇。茹納之內，規畫存焉，俾驕矜者弗敢肆，足矣；保愛之餘，防閑密焉，令怙侈者有所憚，足矣。夫寬行於制之中，而制不出於寬之外，若此者，所以和之也。然政有緩急，不可凌其序而雜施；民有頑淳，不可拂其性而加責。教化未洽，假歲月以摩之，優游浸漬，自然淪浹於肌膚矣；習俗未消，寬程限以率之，馴擾調娛，自然融液於心志矣。謂之曰和，其庶幾乎！至是則孝恭之德已施於政，而馨香之治可感乎神，所以弘正訓、化殷民者至矣，雖周公而在，何以尚茲？抑聞之《傳》曰：「政寬則糾之以猛，政猛則施之以寬，寬以濟猛，猛以濟寬，政是以和。」其說蓋出於此。然所謂猛者，亦有制云爾，豈遂束縛之、馳驟之，若牛馬然乎？即周公謹毖，而云「師保萬民，民懷其德」，似非專任威者。三代聖人享國長久，大都以寬和民。自火烈水弱之說行，而申、韓者流遂以其學禍天下。吁，可鑒也！

《詩》
translation_en:
…grace without discrimination. Within tolerance and acceptance, regulations and plans remain, making it enough so that the arrogant and boastful dare not act wantonly; alongside protection and affection, strict safeguards are maintained, making it enough so that the impenitent and extravagant have something to fear. When leniency operates within regulation, and regulation does not go beyond leniency, doing this is the way to bring them into harmony. Yet governance has matters of urgency and leisure, and one must not overstep their sequence and apply measures haphazardly; the people have both the obstinate and the simple, and one must not go against their nature and heap blame upon them. When moral transformation has not yet taken hold, grant months and years to mold them; through unhurried immersion, it will naturally soak into their very skin and flesh. When old habits and customs have not yet faded, relax the deadlines to lead them; through gentle taming and soothing, it will naturally melt into their hearts and minds. To call this harmony—is it not close to the mark! Reaching this point, the virtues of filial piety and reverence have already been applied to governance, and fragrant rule can move the spirits. The means of ampliarizing the upright teachings and transforming the Yin people have reached the utmost; even if the Duke of Zhou (Zhougong 周公) were alive, how could he surpass this? Moreover, I have heard it said in the Zuo Commentary (Zhuan 傳): "When governance is lenient, rectify it with severity; when governance is severe, temper it with leniency. Leniency complements severity, and severity complements leniency; thus governance is brought into harmony." That theory likely originated from this. Yet what is called "severity" merely means having regulations; how could it mean tying them up and driving them at a gallop like cattle and horses? Even when the Duke of Zhou exercised cautious vigilance, it was said that he "acted as teacher and protector to the myriad people, and the people cherished his virtue," which seems not to have relied exclusively on stern authority. The sages of the Three Dynasties enjoyed long-lasting reigns mostly by harmonizing the people through leniency. Ever since the analogy of fierce fire and weak water gained currency, the likes of Shen Buhai 申不害 and Han Fei 韓非 consequently brought disaster upon the empire with their doctrines. Alas, this should serve as a warning!

Book of Odes (Shi 詩)

translation_en:
"Happiness to our prince, parent of the people! Happiness to our prince, whose virtuous fame is unending!"

Gao Hongmo 高洪謨

Associate Examiner Instructor (jiaoyu) Qiu 丘 comments: Where he expounds upon "parent" and "virtuous fame," he traces them back to the ruler's virtue and the ruler's renown—an original insight. Selected.

Associate Examiner Instructor Xu 徐 comments: Neat, pure, and serenely elegant, and the two concluding sections are especially spirited.

Associate Examiner Instructor Lin 林 comments: The thought is thoroughly integrated and lucid, the tone refined and remarkable; an utterly superb exposition of the Classic of Poetry (Shijing). Selected.

Associate Examiner Instructor (jiaoshou) Xie 謝 comments: Pure, orthodox, and adhering to classical standards; nothing surpasses this essay.

Examiner Expositor-in-waiting (shijiang) Han 韓 comments: Refined and observant of the rules. Selected.

Examiner Left Admonisher (zuo yude) Zhu 朱 comments: Harmoniously integrated and brilliant.

When the true king feasts his guests, he praises both their virtue in drawing near to the people and their virtue in winning enduring renown. For the common people do not constantly cherish someone easily, nor is renown easily sustained for long; without the abundant virtue of the noble man, who could achieve this? Feasting his guests, the king sings: Banquets are indeed a constant institution of the state, and worthy talents are truly an auspicious blessing to the age; how fortunate am I in today's feast to receive the grace of these noble men! Indeed, superiors are those upon whom inferiors rely, and never have superiors been benevolent without inferiors cleaving to them; it is only when virtue falls short that one has no means to be a parent to these people. Now our happy and courteous noble men have perfected their virtue in harmony and ease, and their genial bearing, so well suited to the common people and to all men…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
也以行君令而致之民必有強敎悅安之澤以
宣上德而達之下必有公好公惡之施蓋惟體
仁以長人必不拂衆以從欲故爲民所瞻依而
撫我之尊不啻如生我之親矣我周以父母天
下爲王道何幸而有一德之佐如君子者乎名
者實之賓未有實至而名不孚者惟德之或渝
而始無以永終其譽耳我樂只之君子溫文成
性而藹然爲龍爲光之望也仁聲遐播宜與順
治之譽相無窮義聞日宣宜與威嚴之烈相爲
===
久蓋惟篤實而暉光未始違道以干譽故其德
音日新而光終之吉不替其蚤譽之美矣先王
以令聞不已顯世業何幸而有恒德之輔如君
子者乎吁王者歌此以燕賓其尊之也有道矣
蓋其所稱樂只焉者仁之徵也民之命也譽之
歸也太和在成周宇宙閒其一仁之流溢乎後
世以殘刻厲民而且以獵一時之譽吾不知其
樂只何如也而國奚賴矣噫
保右命之自天申之干祿百福子孫千億

久蓋惟篤實而暉光未始違道以干譽故其德
音日新而光終之吉不替其發譽之美矣先王
以令聞不已顯世業何者而有恒德之輔如君
子者乎吁王者歌此以燕賓其尊之也有道矣
蓋其所稱樂只焉者仁之徵也民之命也譽之
歸也太和在成周宇宙間其一仁之流溢乎後
世以殘刻厲民而且以獮一時之譽吾不知其
樂只何如也而國奚賴矣噫
保右命之自天申之干祿百福子孫千億
punctuated:
也。以行君令而致之民，必有強敎悅安之澤；以宣上德而達之下，必有公好公惡之施。蓋惟體仁以長人，必不拂衆以從欲，故爲民所瞻依，而撫我之尊不啻如生我之親矣。我周以父母天下爲王道，何幸而有一德之佐如君子者乎！名者，實之賓，未有實至而名不孚者，惟德之或渝，而始無以永終其譽耳。我樂只之君子，溫文成性，而藹然爲龍爲光之望也。仁聲遐播，宜與順治之譽相無窮；義聞日宣，宜與威嚴之烈相爲久。蓋惟篤實而暉光，未始違道以干譽，故其德音日新，而光終之吉不替其蚤譽之美矣。先王以令聞不已顯世業，何幸而有恒德之輔如君子者乎！吁！王者歌此以燕賓，其尊之也有道矣。蓋其所稱「樂只」焉者，仁之徵也，民之命也，譽之歸也。太和在成周宇宙閒，其一仁之流溢乎！後世以殘刻厲民，而且以獵一時之譽，吾不知其樂只何如也，而國奚賴矣！噫！

保右命之，自天申之。干祿百福，子孫千億。
translation_en:
… When he carries out the ruler's commands and delivers them to the common people, there are surely the blessings of vigorous instruction and joyful peace; when he proclaims the sovereign's virtue and extends it to those below, there is surely the administration of loving what the public loves and hating what the public hates. Indeed, only because he embodies benevolence to lead men will he never go against the multitude to indulge his own desires; therefore, he is looked up to and relied upon by the people, and the revered one who nurtures us is no different from the parents who gave us birth. Our Zhou dynasty takes being parent to all under Heaven as the Kingly Way—how fortunate to have an assistant of pure, single virtue like this noble man!

Reputation is the guest of reality; never has reality been attained without reputation corresponding to it. Only when virtue perhaps wavers does one first lack the means to preserve one's fame to the very end. Our joyous noble man has a nature formed of gentle refinement, and graciously commands the esteem of being favored and glorious. The renown of his benevolence spreads far, fittingly endless alongside the praise of his harmonious governance; the fame of his righteousness is proclaimed daily, fittingly enduring alongside the splendor of his majestic dignity. Indeed, only because he is sincere, substantial, and brilliantly illustrious has he never violated the Way to seek praise; therefore, his virtuous reputation is daily renewed, and the auspiciousness of a glorious conclusion never diminishes the beauty of his early fame. The Former Kings made their hereditary enterprise illustrious through unceasing good renown—how fortunate to have a helper of constant virtue like this noble man!

Ah! When the true king sings this in feasting his guests, there is a true way in how he honors them. For what he calls "joyous" is the manifestation of benevolence, the life of the people, and the convergence of praise. Supreme harmony filled the universe of the flourishing Zhou—was it not the overflowing of a single benevolence? In later ages, men afflict the people with cruelty and harshness, and yet use this to hunt for momentary praise; I do not know how they could be called "joyous," and what the state could rely upon in them! Alas!

"[The heavens] protect, aid, and appoint him, / From Heaven renewing his mandate. / Seeking emolument, he receives a hundred blessings, / His sons and grandsons in thousands and hundreds of millions."

Nie Yunhan 聶雲翰

Associate Examiner Instructor Qiu 丘 comments: The sentiment of ministers responding in praise is warm and gracious; it is truly suitable to serve as a model.
Associate Examiner Instructor Xu 徐 comments: Precise, fitting, and harmoniously blended. Being an excellent exposition of the Odes (Book of Songs), it is recorded to serve as a model.
Associate Examiner Instructor Lin 林 comments: In their loyal affection for their ruler, ministers leave no stone unturned in reaching the utmost; this composition captures that spirit.
Associate Examiner Instructor Xie 謝 comments: Refined, original, elegant, and unconstrained; standing out far above the crowd.
Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Han 韓 comments: Smooth and well-balanced, matching the elegant meaning of the Ode.
Examiner Left Admonisher Zhu 朱 comments: The language is refined and the meaning is earnest.

Ministers wish for their ruler's blessings to be generously bestowed by Heaven and abundantly bequeathed to posterity. For among blessings, making one's descendants prosperous is the greatest; when a true king's blessings are so supremely generous from Heaven, how could they fail to be abundant for his posterity? The ode "Jia le" 假樂 (Greatly Happy), in responding to the ruler's good will, conveys this meaning: He who possesses virtue will surely be generously favored by Heaven, and in speaking of blessings, what is valued is that they endure for a long time. In our king's admirable joy, his virtue is profound indeed—how could his blessings fail to be long-lasting? For just as the king's virtue shines forth and reaches Heaven unceasingly, so too does the mind of Heaven look upon the king with loving care unceasingly. Heaven protects him to secure his person, assists him to support his actions, and charges him with the Mandate to glorify his enterprise—in thus lavishing favor and peace upon the sovereign's throne, what single aspect is not all-encompassing? Protecting him and repeatedly renewing that protection, assisting him and repeatedly renewing that assistance, charging him and repeatedly renewing that charge—whereby…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
以常敷錫于九重者何一之弗繼也天休帝祉
大來而無方戬穀罄宜日新而無斁吾於是而
知君子之干祿有道矣吾於是而知君子之百
福攸同矣安富尊榮以一身享乎其豐而未已
也天地儲祥錫胤極本支之盛繼君而子繼子
而孫而千億其靡窮也螽斯之蟄蟄曾足以喻
其蕃乎伴奐優游以一時履乎其泰而猶未也
神明啓胄多男衍豐芑之遺子而又孫孫而又
子而千億其未艾也麟趾之振振曾足以限其
===
美乎斯則保右命之申勿替引之而宜民人之
統永世克紹干祿百福孰大于此必如是而荅
稱之願其少遂乎吁公尸之忠愛至矣夫周自
后稷公劉以仁厚立國發祥何長也而後王復
培以宜民人之德則其子孫卜世之長宜矣然
歌假樂者必曰穆穆皇皇曰不懈于位夫使其
世德敬美而居位不懈則周雖至今存可也吾
故曰周臣之忠愛也
春秋

以常敷錫于九重者，何一之弗繼也！天休帝祉，大來而無方；戬穀罄宜，日新而無斁。吾於是而知君子之干祿有道矣，吾於是而知君子之百福攸同矣。安富尊榮，以一身享乎其豐而未已也。天地儲祥，錫胤極本支之盛，繼君而子，繼子而孫，而千億其靡窮也，《螽斯》之蟄蟄，曾足以喻其蕃乎？伴奐優游，以一時履乎其泰而猶未也。神明啓胄，多男衍豐芑之遺，子而又孫，孫而又子，而千億其未艾也，《麟趾》之振振，曾足以限其美乎？斯則保右命之申，勿替引之，而宜民人之統，永世克紹。干祿百福，孰大于此？必如是而荅稱之願，其少遂乎！吁！公尸之忠愛至矣。夫周自后稷、公劉以仁厚立國，發祥何長也！而後王復培以宜民人之德，則其子孫卜世之長，宜矣。然歌《假樂》者，必曰「穆穆皇皇」，曰「不懈于位」。夫使其世德敬美而居位不懈，則周雖至今存可也。吾故曰：周臣之忠愛也。
《春秋》
translation_en:
…in which He constantly bestows His blessings upon the ninefold palace—in which single respect is this not continuously sustained? Heavenly favor and Divine blessings arrive in great measure and without bound; perfection of goodness and complete propriety are daily renewed without weariness. From this I know that the noble man has a true way of seeking emolument; from this I know that in the noble man the hundred blessings all converge!

In peace, wealth, honor, and glory, he enjoys abundance in his own person, and yet it does not stop there. Heaven and Earth store up auspiciousness and bestow posterity, bringing the flourishing of root and branch to the utmost: sons succeeding the ruler, grandsons succeeding the sons, in thousands and hundreds of thousands without end! Could the harmonious clustering in the ode "Locusts" (Zhongsi) ever suffice to serve as a metaphor for such abundance? In relaxed leisure and carefree ease, he treads in prosperity for his own time, and yet that is still not all. The gods and spirits open the way for his descendants, with many sons extending the legacy of the lush white millet: sons followed by grandsons, and grandsons again followed by sons, in thousands and hundreds of thousands without cease! Could the noble vigor in the ode "The Lin's Hooves" (Linzhi) ever suffice to set a limit to such excellence?

This, then, is the renewal of Heaven's protecting, assisting, and mandating him, drawing it out without fail, so that the lineage that rightly orders the common people and the officers can be perpetuated for eternal generations. In seeking emolument and the hundred blessings, what could be greater than this? Only when it is like this can the wish to respond to and extol the sovereign be somewhat fulfilled!

Ah! The loyalty and affection of the impersonator of the dead reached the utmost. Now, from the time Hou Ji and Gong Liu founded the state with benevolence and generosity, how long-lasting was the origin of Zhou's auspiciousness! And when later kings further cultivated it with the virtue that rightly orders the common people and the officers, it was only fitting that the divination of their descendants' generations should be so long. Yet he who sang the ode "Felicitous and Joyous" (Jiale) necessarily said, "Reverent, reverent; august, august," and said, "Never remiss in his position." Now, had they caused their hereditary virtue to remain reverently admirable and never been remiss while occupying the throne, then the Zhou house might well have survived even to this very day. Therefore I say: such was the loyalty and affection of the Zhou ministers.

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
春齊侯伐宋圍緡僖公二十有三年
張我繩
同考試官學正朱批思精而邃筆勁而奇
發傳意剴切明盡卓有大雅風度
考試官侍講韓批精雅謹嚴
考試官左諭德朱批事核詞嚴
伯嗣乗約而虐大國春秋深罪之也夫伯者以
恤患為職患則弗恤又因而重困之斯豈義所
得為哉昔齊侯伐宋討其不與盟于齊也君子
===
曰齊之盟也不曰修好諸侯以無忘桓公之德
乎桓之德在攘夷安夏也在分災善隣也孝也
嗣之第令克纘先猷以輯寧中國豈不赫然稱
義問哉今于泓之敗宋難方殷公股之傷友邦
共恤乃從而伐其國焉環其邑焉此以何名為
兵端也徒謂宋襄圖伯非我之利也茲而見挫
於楚是得逞之時也曾不思幸人之災不仁而
況蠻夷得志詎直一宋人之不幸者顧可伺釁
而恣其暴乎乗人之危不武而況商墟被禍尤

伯嗣乗約而虐大國，《春秋》深罪之也。夫伯者以恤患為職，患則弗恤，又因而重困之，斯豈義所得為哉？昔齊侯伐宋，討其不與盟于齊也。君子曰：齊之盟也，不曰「修好諸侯，以無忘桓公之德」乎？桓之德，在攘夷安夏也，在分災善隣也。孝也嗣之，第令克纘先猷，以輯寧中國，豈不赫然稱義問哉？今于泓之敗，宋難方殷，公股之傷，友邦共恤，乃從而伐其國焉，環其邑焉，此以何名為兵端也？徒謂宋襄圖伯，非我之利也；茲而見挫於楚，是得逞之時也。曾不思幸人之災，不仁；而況蠻夷得志，詎直一宋人之不幸者，顧可伺釁而恣其暴乎？乗人之危，不武；而況商墟被禍，尤
translation_en:
"In spring, the Marquis of Qi invaded Song and laid siege to Min." [Twenty-third Year of Duke Xi]

Zhang Wosheng

Associate Examiner, Confucian School Director (xuezheng) Zhu comments: The thought is refined and profound; the brushwork is vigorous and extraordinary. It brings out the meaning of the commentary incisively, clearly, and exhaustively, possessing the lofty bearing of great elegance.
Examiner, Expositor-in-waiting (shijiang) Han comments: Refined, elegant, and rigorously structured.
Examiner, Left Admonisher (zuo yude) Zhu comments: The facts are verified and the diction is stern.

When the heir of a hegemon takes advantage of another's distress to oppress a great state, the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) deeply condemns him. Now, a hegemon takes relieving disaster as his duty; when there is disaster, if he not only fails to relieve it, but takes the opportunity to compound its distress, how could this be something permissible by righteousness? In the past, the Marquis of Qi invaded Song to punish it for not participating in the covenant at Qi. A gentleman would say: At the covenant of Qi, was it not declared, "Let us cultivate good relations among the feudal lords so as not to forget the virtue of Duke Huan"? The virtue of Huan lay in repelling the barbarians and pacifying the central states; it lay in sharing in disasters and being good to neighbors. When Duke Xiao succeeded him, had he only been able to carry on his predecessor's plans in order to bring harmony and peace to the central states, would he not have won a brilliant reputation for righteousness? Yet now, with the defeat at the Hong River, Song's troubles were at their height, and with the wounding of the Duke's thigh, friendly states all felt compassion—yet Qi thereupon invaded its state and encircled its town. Under what pretext did it initiate hostilities? It was merely the thought that Duke Xiang of Song's ambition to become hegemon was not to Qi's advantage, and that now, having been thwarted by Chu, this was the moment for Qi to have its way. He never stopped to consider that to rejoice in another's misfortune is inhumane—and how much more so when the southern barbarians achieve their ambitions! Is that merely the misfortune of the people of Song alone? How could one watch for an opening and give free rein to one's brutality? To take advantage of another's peril is unmartial—and how much more so when the ruins of Shang suffer calamity, which especially…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
爲繫同室之安危者顧可利難而加之兵乎外
助夷氛之虐內戕親暱之邦人之稱斯師也何
義矣噫救鄭存衛而天下頌德匡合之績猶存
也伐楚次陘而天下稱烈賜履之光未泯也先
公惠及諸姬而今也不能釋一宋先公威振四
夷而今也反以殘中夏伯國之餘業不幾于替
哉經故書伐國而言圍邑以罪之視諸伐鄭圍
新城之書所謂美惡不嫌同詞者也抑孝公之
立襄實爲之彼固儼然有德色矣乃孝也竟以
===
怨報焉此豈人情也哉天下惟德義可以懷人
而私惠不足爲德襄也狥私囑而伐齊喪當時
如邢如狄旣已竊議其後佳兵之報固其所巳
此可爲永鑒巳
六月癸酉季孫行父臧孫許叔孫僑如公
孫嬰齊帥師會晉郤克衛孫良夫曹公
子首及齊侯戰于鞌齊師敗績〔成公二年〕
六月公會單子晉侯宋公衛侯鄭伯
莒子邾子齊世子光已未同盟于雞澤

爲繫同室之安危者，顧可利難而加之兵乎？外助夷氛之虐，內戕親暱之邦，人之稱斯師也，何義矣！噫！救鄭存衛而天下頌德，匡合之績猶存也；伐楚次陘而天下稱烈，賜履之光未泯也。先公惠及諸姬，而今也不能釋一宋；先公威振四夷，而今也反以殘中夏，伯國之餘業，不幾于替哉！經故書伐國而言圍邑以罪之，視諸「伐鄭圍新城」之書，所謂美惡不嫌同詞者也。抑孝公之立，襄實爲之，彼固儼然有德色矣，乃孝也竟以怨報焉，此豈人情也哉？天下惟德義可以懷人，而私惠不足爲德。襄也狥私囑而伐齊喪，當時如邢如狄，旣已竊議其後，佳兵之報，固其所巳，此可爲永鑒巳。

「六月，癸酉，季孫行父、臧孫許、叔孫僑如、公孫嬰齊帥師，會晉郤克、衛孫良夫、曹公子首，及齊侯戰于鞌，齊師敗績。」〔成公二年〕「六月，公會單子、晉侯、宋公、衛侯、鄭伯、莒子、邾子、齊世子光，已未，同盟于雞澤。」
translation_en:
…especially tied to the safety and peril of our fellow states of the same house—how could one instead take advantage of their distress and send troops against them? Externally aiding the savagery of the barbarian menace, and internally harming a closely allied state—when people speak of this campaign, what righteousness is there in it? Alas! Rescuing Zheng and preserving Wei so that all under heaven praised his virtue—the achievements of rectifying and uniting the realm still endured; attacking Chu and halting at Xing so that all under heaven acclaimed his exploits—the glory of the territorial mandate bestowed upon him had not yet faded. The former duke extended his kindness to all the Ji-surnamed states, yet now he cannot even spare Song alone; the former duke made his awe felt among the four barbarian tribes, yet now he instead ravages the central Xia states. Is not the remaining legacy of the hegemonic state nearly ruined? Therefore the Classic records the attack on the state and mentions the siege of the settlement in order to condemn it; compared with the entry "attacked Zheng and besieged Xincheng," this is a case of what is called not shying away from using identical wording for both praiseworthy and blameworthy acts. Moreover, the installation of Duke Xiao was in fact accomplished by Duke Xiang of Song, who certainly bore the proud countenance of a benefactor; yet Xiao ultimately repaid him with enmity—how could this be human feeling? In the world, only virtue and righteousness can win people's hearts, whereas private favors are insufficient to constitute virtue. Because Xiang followed a private behest and attacked Qi during its mourning period, at that time even states like Xing and the Di tribes already privately criticized him behind his back. The retribution for delighting in arms was indeed what he brought upon himself, and this may serve as an eternal warning.

"In the sixth month, on the guiyou day, Jisun Xingfu, Zangsun Xu, Shusun Qiaoru, and Gongsun Yingqi led troops to join Xi Ke of Jin, Sun Liangfu of Wei, and Gongzi Shou of Cao, and fought with the Marquis of Qi at An; the army of Qi was utterly defeated." [Second year of Duke Cheng] "In the sixth month, the Duke met with Viscount Shan, the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, and Heir Apparent Guang of Qi; on the jiwei day, they made a covenant together at Jize." …

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
襄公三年
張我繼
同考試官學正朱批體裁嚴整詞氣偉健
蓋一洗浮蔓獨據心得者也錄之爲士道龜鑑
考試官侍講韓批正大秀抜
考試官左諭德朱批筆力高古
聖人以忠教天下故於辭善不辭過者有取焉
此見卻克之善稱君而魏絳之過稱已可以作
天下忠矣蓋嘗聞君陳之忠焉有嘉謀則曰惟
===
后之德孰意晉臣如卻克亦能明之也鞌之役
晉遣八百賦輿以伐不敬此無論兵興之何如
維時靡笄戰勝克也寔援枹焉威之能震而敵
以摧豈非已之善哉乃克還師而入見則以爲
君之訓臣何力之有儼然歸善于君而不自居
焉語云無成代有終克之意亦猶是矣人臣咸
若時將衆美而効之上庶可以作謙謙不伐之
忠乎又嘗聞伊尹之忠焉有不獲則曰時予之
辜孰意晉臣如魏絳亦能修之也雞澤之役晉

維時靡笄戰勝克也寔援枹焉威之能震而敵
以摧豈非巳之善哉乃克還師而入見則以為
君之訓臣何力之有儼然歸善于君而不自居
焉語云無成代有終克之意亦猶是矣人臣咸
若時恃衆美而効之上庶可以作謙謙不伐之
忠乎又嘗聞伊尹之忠焉有不獲則曰時予之

〔襄公三年〕

聖人以忠教天下，故於辭善不辭過者有取焉。此見卻克之善稱君，而魏絳之過稱已，可以作天下忠矣。蓋嘗聞君陳之忠焉，有嘉謀則曰「惟后之德」，孰意晉臣如卻克亦能明之也！鞌之役，晉遣八百賦輿以伐不敬。此無論兵興之何如，維時靡笄戰勝，克也寔援枹焉。威之能震而敵以摧，豈非已之善哉？乃克還師而入見，則以爲「君之訓，臣何力之有」，儼然歸善于君而不自居焉。語云「無成，代有終」，克之意亦猶是矣。人臣咸若時，將衆美而効之上，庶可以作謙謙不伐之忠乎！又嘗聞伊尹之忠焉，有不獲則曰「時予之辜」，孰意晉臣如魏絳亦能修之也！雞澤之役，晉

Indeed, this thoroughly washes away superficial verbosity and relies solely on personal insight. We record it as a mirror and touchstone for the Way of the scholar."
Examiner Expositor-in-Waiting (shijiang) Han comments: "Upright, grand, refined, and outstanding."
Examiner Left Admonisher (zuo yude) Zhu comments: "The brushwork is lofty and archaic."

The Sage teaches all under Heaven through loyalty, and therefore takes approving note of those who decline credit for what goes well while not declining blame for faults. Herein we see how Xi Ke 卻克 attributed success to his lord, while Wei Jiang 魏絳 attributed the fault to himself—enough to inspire loyalty throughout the world!

Indeed, we have heard of the loyalty of Junchen 君陳: when there was a fine plan, he said, "It is solely the virtue of my sovereign." Who would have thought that a minister of Jin 晉 like Xi Ke could also understand this! In the campaign of An 鞌, Jin dispatched eight hundred levied war chariots to punish disrespect. Setting aside the nature of why troops were raised, when victory was won at Miji 靡笄 at that time, it was truly Ke who grasped the drumstick. That their might shook the enemy and crushed them—was this not his own achievement? Yet when Ke returned with the army and entered for an audience, he held that "it was due to my lord's instruction; what strength did your subject contribute?" Dignified, he attributed the credit to his lord and did not claim it for himself. As the saying goes, "Claiming no completion, yet bringing things to an end on another's behalf"—Ke's intention was just like this. If all ministers were like this, gathering every excellence and presenting it to their superior, might this not inspire a modest and unboastful loyalty?

Again, we have heard of the loyalty of Yi Yin 伊尹: when someone did not attain their proper place, he said, "This is my guilt." Who would have thought that a minister of Jin like Wei Jiang could also practice this! In the campaign of Jize 雞澤, Jin …
