translation_en:
… ordered [今, a graphic error for 令] one or two brother states to consult on those who were uncooperative. Regardless of how the covenant meeting went, at the time when disorder broke out in the ranks at Quliang, it was Wei Jiang who wielded the executioner's axe. That instructions had not been made clear and a close kinsman was indulged—was this not the fault of the ruler? Yet when Jiang handed over his written statement and requested punishment, he considered it his own crime as a minister and dared not anger the ruler's heart, magnanimously taking the blame upon himself without making excuses. The saying goes, "One who eats the ruler's stipend does not shirk difficulty." Jiang's intention was just like this. If all ministers were like this, overcoming difficulties and taking responsibility upon themselves below, might it not foster a loyalty that is steadfast and selfless? As for Hua Yuan and Zifan, they arrogated credit to themselves while exposing their rulers' faults; they are truly sinners compared to these two ministers of Jin! Even so,郤 Ke's (Xi Ke's) achievement is not worth recording; he was merely avenging the grievance of being laughed at. Wei Jiang declined the music of bells and chimes, and in offering praise he did not forget to admonish; truly he possessed the demeanor of a loyal minister. Moreover, if we examine that era, Duke Dao was just then enlightened and not of the same caliber as Duke Jing. Offices did not alter their regular duties, and ranks did not exceed virtue; therefore renowned ministers arose in succession and Jin flourished through them. Speaking from this perspective, if a ruler of men wishes his ministers to practice loyalty in serving their superior, how careful he must be in whom he employs!

Record of Rites (Liji)
"The zither of the 'Pure Temple' (Qingmiao) has vermilion strings and widely spaced sound-holes; one leads the singing and three sigh in response—there is lingering sound in it! The ceremony of the Great Banquet places plain water (xuanjiu) in the seat of honor, puts raw fish on the offering stands, and leaves the great broth unseasoned—there is lingering flavor in it!"
By Zhang Wenxing.

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
音玩之有餘味邃於養者
考試官侍講韓批莊雅典古
考試官左諭德朱批精確
記者徴禮樂之至而有不事乎文焉夫禮樂而
文非其至者也觀清廟之遺音大饗之遺味而
文何爲哉今之言禮樂者尚文而忘本敝也甚
矣吾謂隆樂非極音重禮非致味者蓋維之也
而安所徴邪彼清廟以咏文德至隆樂也使隆
樂而尚極音宜莫如清廟矣今言乎其瑟絃而
===
朱焉越而疏焉一倡而三歎焉此其音質素而
已非極也然元聲未雜而悠然餘響之無窮可
以移風可以易俗聽之者其有遐思乎夫音之
一聽而無餘者道德不足故爾清廟則合道德
之致矣是故德音之音有遺音也大饗以仁祖
考至重禮也使重禮而尚致味宜莫如大饗矣
今言乎其禮尊則玄酒焉俎則腥魚焉大羹則
不和焉此其味質素而已非致也然醇風未漓
而澹然旨趣之有永可以報本可以反始玩之

punctuated:
音，玩之有餘味，邃於養者。
考試官侍講韓批：莊雅典古。
考試官左諭德朱批：精確。

記者徴禮樂之至，而有不事乎文焉。夫禮樂而文，非其至者也。觀《清廟》之遺音、大饗之遺味，而文何爲哉？今之言禮樂者，尚文而忘本，敝也甚矣。吾謂隆樂非極音，重禮非致味者，蓋維之也，而安所徴邪？彼《清廟》以咏文德，至隆樂也；使隆樂而尚極音，宜莫如《清廟》矣。今言乎其瑟，絃而朱焉，越而疏焉，一倡而三歎焉，此其音質素而已，非極也。然元聲未雜，而悠然餘響之無窮，可以移風，可以易俗，聽之者其有遐思乎？夫音之一聽而無餘者，道德不足故爾；《清廟》則合道德之致矣，是故德音之音，有遺音也。大饗以仁祖考，至重禮也；使重禮而尚致味，宜莫如大饗矣。今言乎其禮，尊則玄酒焉，俎則腥魚焉，大羹則不和焉，此其味質素而已，非致也。然醇風未漓，而澹然旨趣之有永，可以報本，可以反始，玩之
translation_en:
… resonance, and upon savoring it, there is a lingering flavor; this is someone profound in self-cultivation.
Examiner and Expositor-in-Waiting Han comments: Dignified, elegant, classical, and antique.
Examiner and Left Admonisher Zhu comments: Precise and exact.

The compiler of the Record adduces the perfection of ritual and music, showing that it does not busy itself with outward embellishment. Now, when ritual and music become mere embellishment, they are not at their perfection. When one observes the lingering resonance of the "Pure Temple" (Qingmiao) and the lingering flavor of the Great Banquet, what need is there for embellishment? Those who speak of ritual and music today prize embellishment and forget the fundamental, which is a grave corruption indeed! When I say that the grandest music does not lie in the most extreme sounds, and the weightiest ritual does not lie in the most exquisite flavors, it is to uphold this principle—and by what may we verify it?

That "Pure Temple" hymn, sung in praise of King Wen's virtue, is the grandest of music. If the grandest music prized extreme sound, nothing ought to surpass the "Pure Temple." Yet when we speak of its zithers, the strings are of boiled red silk, the sound-holes are wide and far apart, and when one leads the chant, three sigh in response. Such sound is simply plain and unadorned, not pushed to the extreme. Yet the primal note remains unmixed, and its far-reaching, lingering echoes are inexhaustible—capable of transforming the風 (winds/influences) and changing customs. Must not those who hear it be moved to distant thoughts? When a sound is heard once and leaves nothing lingering, it is because moral virtue is lacking; the "Pure Temple," however, accords with the utmost of moral virtue, and therefore the sound of virtuous music has a lingering resonance.

The Great Banquet, through which benevolence is shown to the ancestral forefathers, is the weightiest of rituals. If the weightiest ritual prized exquisite flavor, nothing ought to surpass the Great Banquet. Yet when we speak of its ritual vessels and offerings, in the goblets there is only dark water, on the sacrificial stands there is raw fish, and the great broth is unseasoned. Such flavor is simply plain and unadorned, not brought to exquisite perfection. Yet pure customs have not yet grown thin, and its tranquil meaning and savor are enduring—capable of repaying the root and returning to the beginning. Those who savor it…

translation_en:
… savor them be moved to far-reaching reflections? When flavors are savored once and leave nothing lingering behind, it is because sincerity and reverence are insufficient. The Great Banquet, however, possesses in full the virtue of sincerity and reverence; therefore, the flavor of the ultimate flavor leaves a lingering savor behind. Ah! When the gentleman examines this, he can set his mind upon the fundamental. Moreover, in the affairs of the world, one begins by returning from refinement to simplicity, and then proceeds from simplicity to refinement; when refinement prevails and the fundamental substance is swept away, this is true not only of rites and music. Thus Confucius wished to reduce the refinement of Zhou and follow the忠 (good faith) of Xia, and whenever anyone was able to investigate the root of the rites, he invariably praised and magnified them. Alas! His inclination can be known indeed. Even with this set up as a dike, there were still those with their "Chamber Music" (Fangzhong) and rope-and-straw rehearsals (mianzui) who claimed that rites and music could thereby be revived!

"The gentleman does not exhaust all profit, so as to leave some for the people."

Zhang Woci
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Gong: The meaning is earnest and sincere, the diction and intent pure and refined. At the end it places the weight on frugality, which is especially an argument that probes the root.
Comment by Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Han: Pure, elegant, grave, and dignified.
Comment by Examiner Left Admonisher Zhu: The essay bears on matters of consequence; record it.

When the gentleman shares profit publicly with the people, his heart of loving nurture is comprehensive indeed. Now, profit is that by which the people profit; if it is exhausted, there is nothing left to leave for the people—and would a gentleman do such a thing? Furthermore, as for the profit present in the world, how could it merely be to supply the uses of the ruler above? Rather, it is also meant to be left for the people; yet if the ruler above instead takes it all and leaves nothing behind, the people cannot bear it. As for the gentleman, because the needs of the military and the state…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之需給之于民固不能不取以經用而億兆之
命懸之于我又不忍盡取以病民斂之以九賦
也而常若不敢盡其賦此何心邪縮吾之入以
寬彼之出而爲吾所寬者穰穰乎其有遺利也
供之以什一也而常若不敢盡其供此何心邪
節吾之取以留彼之資而爲吾所留者熙熙乎
其有遺蓄也天下之財不在官則在民盡之徒
以利吾國矣如民何故有所用有所緩而征戒
其急者正欲貽斯民以富爾而羣黎百姓孰不
===
食君子之餘哉天下之利不在下則在上盡之
徒以益乎上矣如下何故可以取可以無取而
斂從其薄者正欲遺斯民以足爾而四海蒼生
孰不歌君子之賜哉彼先王之世上未嘗不取
而取不見其苛民未嘗不供而供不見其竭其
率用此與雖然有本焉節儉是已蓋取之與用
恒相視者也浮則浮約則約未有儉主而取民
無制者未有奢主而取民有制者周禮經國裕
民之書也而九式節財用詳哉乎其言之於乎

之需給之于民固不能不取以經用而億兆之
命懸之于我又不忍盡取以病民歛之以九賦
也而常若不敢盡其賦此何心邪縮吾之入以
寛彼之出而爲吾所寛者穰穰乎其有遺利也
供之以什一也而常若不敢盡其供此何心邪
節吾之取以留彼之資而爲吾所留者熈熈乎
其有遺蓄也天下之財不在官則在民盡之徒
以利吾國矣如民何故有所用有所緩而征戒
其急者正欲貽斯民以富爾而羣黎百姓孰不

punctuated: 之需給之于民，固不能不取以經用；而億兆之命懸之于我，又不忍盡取以病民。斂之以九賦也，而常若不敢盡其賦，此何心邪？縮吾之入以寬彼之出，而爲吾所寬者，穰穰乎其有遺利也；供之以什一也，而常若不敢盡其供，此何心邪？節吾之取以留彼之資，而爲吾所留者，熙熙乎其有遺蓄也。天下之財，不在官則在民。盡之，徒以利吾國矣，如民何？故有所用、有所緩，而征戒其急者，正欲貽斯民以富爾。而羣黎百姓，孰不食君子之餘哉！天下之利，不在下則在上。盡之，徒以益乎上矣，如下何？故可以取、可以無取，而斂從其薄者，正欲遺斯民以足爾。而四海蒼生，孰不歌君子之賜哉！彼先王之世，上未嘗不取，而取不見其苛；民未嘗不供，而供不見其竭，其率用此與！雖然，有本焉，節儉是已。蓋取之與用，恒相視者也，浮則浮，約則約。未有儉主而取民無制者，未有奢主而取民有制者。《周禮》，經國裕民之書也，而九式節財用，詳哉乎其言之！於乎，
translation_en: …and national needs are supplied by the people, so he certainly cannot avoid taking from them to fund regular expenditures; yet because the lives of the millions hang upon us, he also cannot bear to take everything and thereby distress the people. When he collects from them through the Nine Levies (jiufu), he always acts as though he dares not exhaust those levies—what mind is this? By curtailing our own income in order to ease their outlays, that which we have spared leaves them with an abundant surplus of profit. When they contribute through the one-tenth tithe, he always acts as though he dares not exhaust their contributions—what mind is this? By moderating our exactions in order to leave them their resources, that which we have left them allows them to enjoy a prosperous surplus of savings. The wealth of the world, if not with the officials, is with the people. To exhaust it serves merely to profit our state, yet what becomes of the people? Therefore, where some needs are met and others deferred, and where one guards against urgency in taxation, the intent is precisely to bequeath wealth to these people. And among the multitudes of the common folk, who then does not eat from the surplus left by the noble man! The profit of the world, if not with those below, is with those above. To exhaust it serves merely to benefit those above, yet what becomes of those below? Therefore, when it is questionable whether to take or not to take, and one follows the lighter course in collection, the intent is precisely to leave sufficiency to these people. And among the living souls within the four seas, who then does not sing the praises of the noble man's bounty! In the age of the former kings, superiors never failed to take from the people, yet their taking did not appear harsh; the people never failed to contribute, yet their contributing did not appear to leave them depleted—was it not because they consistently followed this principle? Even so, there is a root to this: namely, frugality. For taking and spending always correspond to one another; if one is extravagant, the other is extravagant, and if one is restrained, the other is restrained. There has never been a frugal ruler who took from the people without limit, nor has there ever been an extravagant ruler who took from the people with restraint. The Rites of Zhou (Zhouli) is a book on governing the state and enriching the people, and how detailed are its words on regulating financial expenditure through the Nine Formulas (jiushi)! Ah,…

第貳場
論
聖王求任輔相爲先
張我繩

同考試官學正朱批：蘊藉春融，才思秀發。不事雕琢，而操縱闔闢，精采燁然。非學識超卓之士不能及此，宜錄以式。
考試官侍講韓批：議論正大，體格平雅。所言極有關係，末知歸重，尤見確識。錄之。

聖王以心治天下，必有所𠯁寄其心者，而後可以善治于不窮。夫天下至大矣，天下之任至艱重矣。聖王者，天所畀以膺艱重之任，而臨至大之勢，非予之以可娛而已也，故必皇皇焉運治也以心。然使其心或先務之弗知，體要之弗執，欲恃其獨智以當紛綸轇轕之衝，盡天下而置
translation_en:
… know the fundamental!

Second Session
Discourse
"The sage-king makes seeking and appointing assisting ministers his priority."
Zhang Wosheng 張我繩

Associate Examiner, Directorate of Education Instructor (xuezheng) Zhu comments: Profound, restrained, and harmonious as spring, with talent and thought blooming brilliantly. Without resorting to artificial carving and polishing, its control, opening, and closing shine with splendor. None but a scholar of surpassing learning and insight could achieve this; it should be recorded as a model.
Examiner, Expositor-in-Waiting (shijiang) Han comments: The argument is upright and grand, the style balanced and elegant. What it says is of utmost consequence, and at the end it knows where to place the ultimate emphasis, which especially shows sound judgment. Record it.
Examiner, Left Admonisher (zuo yude) Zhu comments: It elucidates the meaning of "seeking and appointing" thoroughly, while its style and tone are upright and refined, naturally distinct from those who indulge in unbridled and superficial华iness. It may serve as a model.

A sage-king governs all under Heaven with his mind, yet there must be those sufficient to whom he can entrust his mind, and only afterward can he achieve good governance inexhaustibly. Now, all under Heaven is vast indeed, and the responsibility for all under Heaven is arduous and heavy indeed. A sage-king is one upon whom Heaven has bestowed the charge to shoulder this arduous and heavy responsibility and to preside over a realm of the utmost vastness—it is not given to him merely for his own enjoyment! Therefore, he must anxiously and tirelessly operate his governance through his mind. Yet if his mind should fail to know the foremost tasks, or fail to grasp the essential substance, and he wishes to rely on his solitary wisdom to confront the press of tangled and complex affairs, attempting to take all under Heaven in its entirety and place…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之所其勢不能也於是旁求之天下焉惟其人
可以屬吾倚毗而寄吾願治之心者立之爲相
俾之交修共濟以先天下之理夫是以要而易
達逸而有成盛美溢于當世而治效流于無窮
也嗟乎相道得而天下治矣程子謂古之聖王
未嘗不以求任輔相爲先其以此乎嘗讀易至
于泰曰后以裁成天地之道輔相天地之宜以
左右民其治大矣而其用乃由九二以中行之
臣上應六五虛中下交之君相與而成泰是故
===
觀于泰而聖王治天下之理見矣夫君臣相遇
自古爲難蓋以九重之貴四海之富仰有威命
靈爽之尊而俯有臣妾億兆之勢意指色授天
下之人且奔走竭蹶以奉之不暇而何所賴于
臣第以天下大器民物重任其事繁且夥矣君
人者將邃宇玄希夷默然兀然聽其自理乎則
天下之望我者謂何而奚以爲治抑將焦思雕
慮攉德塞性日斤斤憧憧求天下而登之理乎
則吾亦自不勝其煩而又奚以爲治是故聖王

則吾亦自不勝其煩而又奚以爲治是故聖王
punctuated: 之所，其勢不能也。於是旁求之天下焉，惟其人可以屬吾倚毗、而寄吾願治之心者，立之爲相，俾之交修共濟，以先天下之理。夫是以要而易達，逸而有成，盛美溢于當世，而治效流于無窮也。嗟乎！相道得而天下治矣。程子謂「古之聖王未嘗不以求任輔相爲先」，其以此乎！嘗讀《易》至于《泰》，曰：「后以裁成天地之道，輔相天地之宜，以左右民。」其治大矣！而其用乃由九二以中行之臣，上應六五虛中下交之君，相與而成泰。是故觀于《泰》，而聖王治天下之理見矣。夫君臣相遇，自古爲難。蓋以九重之貴，四海之富，仰有威命靈爽之尊，而俯有臣妾億兆之勢；意指色授，天下之人且奔走竭蹶以奉之不暇，而何所賴于臣？第以天下大器，民物重任，其事繁且夥矣。君人者，將邃宇玄、希夷默然兀然聽其自理乎？則天下之望我者謂何，而奚以爲治？抑將焦思雕慮，攉德塞性，日斤斤憧憧求天下而登之理乎？則吾亦自不勝其煩，而又奚以爲治？是故聖王
translation_en:
… in its proper place, by the nature of things it would be impossible. Therefore, he searches widely throughout the realm: only when he finds a person to whom he can entrust his reliance and assistance, and in whom he can lodge his mind that desires good governance, does he establish him as chief minister, causing them to cultivate virtue together and work in concert so as to put first the ordering of the realm. Because of this, governance is essential yet easy to achieve, effortless yet successful; resplendent excellence brims over in the present age, and the efficacy of rule flows on without end. Alas! When the way of the chief minister is realized, the realm is well governed. When Master Cheng (Cheng Yi 程頤) said, "The sage-kings of antiquity never failed to make seeking and appointing assisting ministers their first priority," was it not for this reason?

I have read the Book of Changes (Yi 易) up to the hexagram "Peace" (Tai 泰), which says: "The ruler thereby regulates and completes the Way of heaven and earth, and assists the suitability of heaven and earth, so as to aid the people." Great indeed is such governance! Yet its operation actually comes about because the minister at Nine in the Second place, walking the middle path, responds above to the ruler at Six in the Fifth place, who with an open mind humbles himself to commune below; together they bring about Peace. Therefore, by observing "Peace," the principle by which the sage-king governs the realm becomes manifest.

Now, the congenial meeting of ruler and minister has since antiquity been difficult. For with the nobility of the ninefold palace and the wealth of the four seas, looking up he possesses the veneration of awe-inspiring mandates and numinous majesty, and looking down he holds the power to make subjects and servants of the myriad millions. At the slightest hint of his wish or expression of his countenance, the people of the realm rush about until they stumble, scarcely having time enough to serve him—what need, then, has he to rely upon ministers? It is only that the realm is a great vessel and the people and things are a heavy responsibility, whose affairs are both complex and numerous. Shall the ruler of men dwell in deep halls and dark mystery [?], in silent and motionless abstraction leaving things to govern themselves? Then what would become of the hopes the realm places in him, and how could he achieve good governance? Or shall he burn his thoughts and carve up his anxieties, uprooting his virtue and stifling his nature, day after day fretfully and restlessly seeking to raise the whole realm to order? Then he himself would be unable to bear the vexation, and how, again, could he achieve good governance? Therefore, the sage-king …

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
有所宜先焉先者得則天下之大可不勞而治
也何也天下之事以一人而應一人則裕以一
人而應千百人則勞以一人而應億兆人則窮
勢也聖王知其然故不以身治天下而以人治
天下以人治天下所謂寄其心者也而其道自
裕矣昔者堯之於唐汲汲以求任乎舜舜之於
虞汲汲以求任禹臯陶孟子稱之曰爲天下得
人者謂之仁而他日又曰堯舜之仁急親賢也
嗚呼是可謂知先天下而聖于理矣自今觀之
===
古之論相而共圖理者何弗先也未得其人則
求旣得其人則任是故衢訪岳咨枚卜吉從擇
之何其愼也詢事考言諸艱歷試知之何其明
也而猶未也懋德嘉績蕨志僉謀信之何其篤
也眾口勿間膠漆不移任之何其專也朝而不
名坐而論道造膝而密語禮之又何厚也舉國
以聽之恭巳以委之吏事不責文例不煩責之
又何重也夫惟如是故爲人君者穆然執要於
上而宰相者惕然殫忠畢智以宣力于下是故

嗚呼是可謂知先天下而聖于理矣自今觀之
===

punctuated: 有所宜先焉。先者得，則天下之大，可不勞而治也。何也？天下之事，以一人而應一人則裕，以一人而應千百人則勞，以一人而應億兆人則窮，勢也。聖王知其然，故不以身治天下，而以人治天下。以人治天下，所謂寄其心者也，而其道自裕矣。昔者堯之於唐，汲汲以求任乎舜；舜之於虞，汲汲以求任禹、臯陶。孟子稱之曰：「爲天下得人者謂之仁。」而他日又曰：「堯、舜之仁，急親賢也。」嗚呼！是可謂知先天下而聖于理矣。自今觀之，古之論相而共圖理者，何弗先也？未得其人則求，旣得其人則任。是故衢訪岳咨，枚卜吉從，擇之何其愼也！詢事考言，諸艱歷試，知之何其明也！而猶未也，懋德嘉績，蕨志僉謀，信之何其篤也！眾口勿間，膠漆不移，任之何其專也！朝而不名，坐而論道，造膝而密語，禮之又何厚也！舉國以聽之，恭巳以委之，吏事不責，文例不煩，責之又何重也！夫惟如是，故爲人君者穆然執要於上，而宰相者惕然殫忠畢智以宣力于下。是故
translation_en: …have what ought to be put first. When that which comes first is attained, the vastness of All-under-Heaven can be governed without toil. Why is this so? In the affairs of the world, for one person to respond to one person is effortless; for one person to respond to hundreds or thousands is toilsome; for one person to respond to millions and billions is exhausting—such is the nature of circumstances. The sage-kings knew this to be so; therefore they did not govern the world through their own persons, but governed the world through other men. Governing the world through other men is what was meant by "entrusting one's mind," and by this Way there is natural abundance. In antiquity, Yao in Tang was anxiously intent on seeking out and employing Shun; Shun in Yu was anxiously intent on seeking out and employing Yu and Gao Yao. Mencius praised this, saying, "To find a man for the empire is called benevolence." And on another day he also said, "The benevolence of Yao and Shun was urgent in becoming intimate with the worthy." Alas! This may indeed be called knowing what to put first in the world and being sagely in governance. Looking at it from the present, in antiquity, when discussing chief ministers with whom to jointly plan governance, how was this not put first? Before obtaining the man, one sought him out; once having obtained the man, one entrusted him with office. Therefore, inquiring in the thoroughfares and consulting the Four Peaks, divining one by one and following the auspicious—how cautious was their selection! Inquiring into affairs and examining words, testing them through all manner of difficulties—how clear was their understanding of them! And yet that was not all: commending their virtue and praising their achievements, fixing their resolve and consulting with all [?]—how earnest was their trust in them! Letting no popular chatter drive a wedge between them, steadfast as glue and lacquer—how exclusive was the responsibility placed in them! Receiving them at court without calling them by personal name, having them sit to discourse upon the Way, drawing close knee-to-knee for confidential counsel—how generous too was the courtesy shown them! Handing the whole state over to heed their counsel, reverently composing oneself to delegate to them, not holding them to petty clerkly duties nor troubling them with bureaucratic precedents—how weighty too was the charge laid upon them! Only because it was thus did the ruler of men sit in solemn dignity holding the essentials above, while the chief minister vigilantly exhausted his loyalty and spent all his wisdom in exerting his strength below. Therefore…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
君都而臣俞不以爲諂君逸而臣勞不以爲怨
推心腹借顔色略忌諱而不以爲僭天子曰是
宰相曰非天子曰可宰相曰否而不以爲亢君
曰爾輔台德爾總朕師臣曰謀猷惟后威福惟
辟而不以爲比君臣之間心神交合以共圖化
理君以此而期之相相亦以此而效之君譬之
人身元首居上而股肱居下股肱不愛其力以
奉元首則精神常運而一身治輔相不隱其忠
以贊一人則德意常孚而天下治是以聖王在
===
上不偏觀望而明被九圍不殫傾耳而聰徹羣
隱不降階序而遐陬遠澨之運化祇德捷于影
響是遵何術哉以相道得而主職舉也故曰人
主之職在論相而已求之而不得其人則用不
效得其人而不善任之則用亦不效嗟乎求任
輔相莫聖王若矣是道也程子舉而歸之商之
高宗何也蓋商自中葉賞僭刑濫外叛內攜幾
于不振矣高宗思中興之業非人莫輔也於是
恭默而求求而夢夢而得一旦以荒野版築之

理君以此而期之相相亦以此而効之君譬之

奉元首則精神常運而一身治輔相不隱其忠
以賛一人則德意常孚而天下治是以聖王在

上不徧覯望而明被九圍不殫傾耳而聰徹羣
隱不降堦序而遐陬遠澨之運化祇德捷于影
響是適何術哉以相道得而主職舉也故曰人
主之職在論相而已求之而不得其人則用不
效得其人而不善任之則用亦不效嗟乎求任
輔相莫聖王若矣是道也程子嘗擧而歸之商之
高宗何也蓋商自中葉賞僭刑濫外叛内攜幾
于不振矣高宗思中興之業非人莫輔也於是
恭默而求求而夢夢而得一旦以荒野版築之
punctuated: 君都而臣俞，不以爲諂；君逸而臣勞，不以爲怨；推心腹，借顔色，略忌諱，而不以爲僭；天子曰「是」，宰相曰「非」，天子曰「可」，宰相曰「否」，而不以爲亢；君曰「爾輔台德，爾總朕師」，臣曰「謀猷惟后，威福惟辟」，而不以爲比。君臣之間，心神交合，以共圖化理。君以此而期之相，相亦以此而效之君。譬之人身，元首居上而股肱居下，股肱不愛其力以奉元首，則精神常運而一身治；輔相不隱其忠以贊一人，則德意常孚而天下治。是以聖王在上，不偏觀望而明被九圍，不殫傾耳而聰徹羣隱，不降階序而遐陬遠澨之運化祇德捷于影響。是遵何術哉？以相道得而主職舉也。故曰「人主之職在論相而已」。求之而不得其人，則用不效；得其人而不善任之，則用亦不效。嗟乎！求任輔相，莫聖王若矣。是道也，程子舉而歸之商之高宗，何也？蓋商自中葉，賞僭刑濫，外叛內攜，幾于不振矣。高宗思中興之業非人莫輔也，於是恭默而求，求而夢，夢而得，一旦以荒野版築之
translation_en: …when the ruler exclaims in praise and the minister assents, it is not considered flattery; when the ruler enjoys ease and the minister toils, it is not considered grounds for resentment; when the ruler extends his utmost confidence, lends a welcoming countenance, and dispenses with taboos, it is not considered presumption; when the Son of Heaven says "Right" and the Prime Minister says "Wrong," or the Son of Heaven says "Permissible" and the Prime Minister says "Impermissible," it is not considered recalcitrance; and when the ruler says, "You shall assist my virtue, you shall command my hosts," and the minister says, "Counsels and plans belong solely to the sovereign, authority to punish and reward belongs solely to the monarch," it is not considered partisan collusion. Between ruler and minister, minds and spirits commune in harmony as they jointly plan for transformative governance. The ruler looks to his Prime Minister with these expectations, and the Prime Minister likewise devotes himself to his ruler in this spirit. It is like the human body, where the head resides above and the limbs below: when the limbs do not spare their strength in serving the head, vital spirit circulates constantly and the whole body is in order; when the assisting Prime Minister does not hold back his loyalty in aiding the One Man, virtuous intentions inspire constant trust and the whole empire is well governed. Therefore, when a sage-king is above, he does not need to peer about everywhere, yet his illumination reaches the nine circuits of the realm; he does not need to strain his ears, yet his acute hearing penetrates all hidden matters; he does not need to descend the palace steps, yet the furthest corners and remotest shores are transformed and brought to revere virtue more swiftly than a shadow follows a form or an echo follows a sound. By what art is this achieved? It is because the Way of the Prime Minister is realized and the duty of the sovereign is fulfilled. Thus it is said: "The duty of the sovereign lies solely in selecting a Prime Minister." If he seeks one and fails to find the right man, the employment will bear no fruit; if he finds the right man but fails to entrust him properly with responsibility, the employment will likewise bear no fruit. Alas! In seeking out and entrusting an assisting Prime Minister, none could match the sage-kings. Why did Master Cheng (Cheng Yi 程頤) single out this Way and attribute it to Gaozong 高宗 of the Shang dynasty? Indeed, from its middle period onward, rewards in the Shang had become excessive and punishments abusive; with rebellion abroad and disaffection within, the dynasty had nearly fallen into irremediable decline. Gaozong reflected that the enterprise of dynastic revival could not be assisted without the right man. Thereupon, in reverent silence he sought him; seeking him, he dreamed of him; dreaming of him, he found him—and in a single morning, took a man of the wilderness laboring at rammed-earth walls…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
夫舉天下而委畀之交修共濟若舟楫鹽梅霖
雨須之急焉卒之嘉靖殷邦還于湯舊則相傅
說之效也嗟乎晚近世之君德不齊夫往昔智
不越夫當世乃徒任其私智慕總攬之名而不
知任相至於政叢務弛左右顧而莫為應卒之
決裂潰敗然後諉罪其臣而無及于事間有不
自親事恣睢任人者矣而相匪其人徒取充位
乃益厚于身謀而薄于國計依違淟涊摸稜取
容以苟旦夕而天下事去矣將鼎折餗覆棟撓
===
榱壓之不支而何共理之有故惟高宗而後為
聖王之求任輔相也雖然賢相所以能輔天下
之治者不徒以其任也以其道也君舉天下而
任之不以為疑天下見其受任之大也亦遂傾
耳注目想望太平惟其所為而莫有不信則其
素所重于天下者必有在矣昔孟子論臣品甚
卑容悅而進之為社稷臣又進之為天民又推
極之則為大人夫大人者正己而物正者也嗚
呼道必大人而後無愧于輔相也已

壞壓之不支而何共理之有故惟高宗而後爲
聖王之求任輔相也雖然賢相所以能輔天下
之治者不徒以其任也以其道也君擧天下而
任之不以爲疑天下見其受任之大也亦遂傾
耳注目想望太平惟其所爲而莫有不信則其
素所重于天下者必有在矣昔孟子論臣品甚
卑容悅而進之爲社稷臣又進之爲天民又推
極之則爲大人夫大人者正己而物正者也嗚
呼道必大人而後無愧于輔相也已
punctuated: 夫，舉天下而委畀之，交修共濟，若舟楫、鹽梅、霖雨，須之急焉。卒之嘉靖殷邦，還于湯舊，則相傅說之效也。嗟乎！晚近世之君，德不齊夫往昔，智不越夫當世，乃徒任其私智，慕總攬之名，而不知任相；至於政叢務弛，左右顧而莫為應，卒之決裂潰敗，然後諉罪其臣，而無及于事。間有不自親事、恣睢任人者矣，而相匪其人，徒取充位，乃益厚于身謀而薄于國計，依違淟涊，摸稜取容，以苟旦夕，而天下事去矣。將鼎折餗覆、棟撓榱壓之不支，而何共理之有？故惟高宗而後為聖王之求任輔相也。雖然，賢相所以能輔天下之治者，不徒以其任也，以其道也。君舉天下而任之，不以為疑；天下見其受任之大也，亦遂傾耳注目，想望太平，惟其所為而莫有不信，則其素所重于天下者，必有在矣。昔孟子論臣品，甚卑容悅，而進之為社稷臣，又進之為天民，又推極之則為大人。夫大人者，正己而物正者也。嗚呼！道必大人，而後無愧于輔相也已。
translation_en: … laborer, he took the entire realm and entrusted it to him. Cultivating virtue together and working in mutual support, he needed him as urgently as one needs boat and oars, salt and plum, or timely rain. In the end, he brought peace and order to the state of Yin and restored it to the former glory of Tang; such was the efficacy of making Fu Yue his chief minister. Alas! Rulers of recent ages have virtue that does not equal that of antiquity and wisdom that does not surpass that of their own generation. Yet they merely rely on their own private cleverness, coveting the reputation of holding all power in their own hands, while not knowing how to entrust responsibility to a chief minister. When it comes to the point where administrative affairs pile up and duties fall into neglect, they look left and right with no one to respond; finally, when things rupture and collapse in ruin, only then do they shift the blame onto their ministers, when it is too late to help matters. Occasionally there are those who do not personally attend to affairs and arbitrarily entrust them to others; yet the chief minister is not the right man and merely fills a post. Thus he becomes ever more generous in scheming for himself and slight in planning for the state—wavering and sullied, hedging to curry favor so as to get by from day to day—and the affairs of the realm are lost. When the tripod's leg breaks and its food is spilled, when the ridgepole bends and the rafters crush down beyond support, what shared governance can there be? Therefore, only with Gaozong do we see a sage king's seeking and employing a chief minister. Even so, the reason a worthy chief minister is able to assist in governing the realm lies not merely in his appointment, but in his Way. When the ruler takes the entire realm and entrusts it to him without entertaining doubt, and the realm, seeing the greatness of the charge he has received, thereupon inclines its ears and fixes its eyes, eagerly hoping for great peace, following whatever he does without anyone failing to trust him—then there must already be something in him that has long commanded the respect of the realm. In the past, when Mencius discussed the grades of ministers, he held in great contempt those who merely seek to please and be favored, and advanced beyond them to the ministers of the altars of soil and grain, advanced further to the people of Heaven, and pushed to the ultimate to reach the great man. Now, a great man is one who rectifies himself and thereby rectifies others. Alas! Only when one's Way is that of a great man can one be worthy, without shame, of being a chief minister.

表

擬宋侍講張栻進講《周南·葛覃》章，因衍其義進規表〔乾道七年〕

張問行

同考試官學正龔批：文王后妃之化，未易形容。是作摹寫《周南·葛覃》景象，勤儉孝敬之風，宛然親炙其盛。且箴規祝願之意，尤見忠藎。謹錄以式。
考試官侍講韓批：清新雋麗，四六之絶佳者。
考試官左諭德朱批：鋪敘有體，且得進規之意，錄之。

乾道七年某月某日，侍講臣栻恭詣崇政殿進講《周南·葛覃》章，謹衍其義爲說上進者。伏以：風行南國，明章著王敎之端；天敞西清，儆戒闡聖經之奥。播遺芬于彤管，可興可觀；炳精義于丹書，以規以諷。竊惟風火《家人》之象，男正外、女正内以交修；農桑衣食之源，帝親耕、后親蠶其唯謹。粤稽
translation_en:
Memorial

A Memorial in Imitation of Expositor-in-waiting Zhang Shi 張栻 of the Song Lecturing on the "Ge Tan" (Spreading Kudzu) Ode of the "Zhou Nan" (Odes of Zhou and the South), Expanding upon Its Meaning to Offer Admonition [Seventh Year of the Qiandao Era (1171)]

Zhang Wenxing 張問行

Comment by Associate Examiner and School Director Gong 龔: The transforming influence of King Wen and his consort is not easy to describe. This composition depicts the scenes of the "Ge Tan" in the "Zhou Nan," and the ethos of diligence, frugality, filial piety, and reverence is as vivid as if one were personally witnessing its flourishing. Moreover, its intent of admonition and good wishes especially shows loyal devotion. Respectfully recorded as a model.
Comment by Examiner and Expositor-in-waiting Han 韓: Fresh, refined, and elegant—an absolutely superb piece of parallel prose.
Comment by Examiner and Left Admonisher Zhu 朱: The exposition has proper form and captures the intent of offering admonition. Record it.

On a certain day of a certain month in the seventh year of the Qiandao era, Your Servant Shi, Expositor-in-waiting, respectfully went to the Chongzheng Palace to lecture on the "Ge Tan" ode of the "Zhou Nan," and respectfully expanded upon its meaning to compose an explanation for presentation to the throne.

Humbly I reflect: As the wind moves across the southern states, luminous chapters manifest the beginning of kingly instruction; as Heaven opens the Western Clear apartments of the palace, admonitions elucidate the profundities of the sage's classics. Spreading the lingering fragrance from the red brush of the female historians, they can inspire and can be observed; illuminating the essential meanings in the cinnabar books, they serve to admonish and to remonstrate.

I venture to reflect that in the image of wind and fire in the "Jia Ren" (The Family) hexagram, the man corrects the outside and the woman corrects the inside in mutual cultivation; as for the source of farming, sericulture, clothing, and food, the Emperor personally plows and the Empress personally tends silkworms with utmost care. Examining into antiquity, …

text:
三代治莫盛於周文厥有二南德首刑于
太姒關關河上方諧荇菜之求莫莫谷中
遂應葛覃之候攬青煙于柔蔓囀黃鳥于
繁陰更刈濩而手自調成爲絺綌而情深
愛惜薄汙薄澣非無文綺之華一縷一絲
盡出經綸之緒侍于君子儼象服以相從
正是國人紛素絲其顧化美哉始基之業
唯季札獨觀其深洋乎盈耳之聲非師摯

既斁匡衡之抗疏徒勤君志已荒太液之

未遇其時恭惟

punctuated: 三代，治莫盛於周文，厥有二南，德首刑于太姒。關關河上，方諧荇菜之求；莫莫谷中，遂應葛覃之候。攬青煙于柔蔓，囀黃鳥于繁陰。更刈濩而手自調，成爲絺綌而情深愛惜。薄汙薄澣，非無文綺之華；一縷一絲，盡出經綸之緒。侍于君子，儼象服以相從；正是國人，紛素絲其顧化。美哉！始基之業，唯季札獨觀其深；洋乎！盈耳之聲，非師摯孰鳴其盛？嗣徽音之云邈，慨純懿其罔宣。鄭聲間奏於房中，新語前稱於馬上。宫彞既斁，匡衡之抗疏徒勤；君志已荒，太液之橫經何益？是皆言而不適於用，亦由生之未遇其時。恭惟〇〇〇〇，至德淵微，大經秩敘。敦孝思而不匱，勅天命以惟幾。
translation_en: … among the Three Dynasties, governance was never more flourishing than under King Wen of Zhou; thus there were the Two Nan odes, in which moral example began with his queen, Tai Si. With the ospreys crying "guan-guan" upon the river, the quest for water-mallow was first harmonized; as the vines grew thick and lush in the valley, the season for the spreading kudzu was answered in turn. Gathering the green mist of the supple vines while yellow orioles warbled in the dense shade, she went on to cut and boil them, preparing them with her own hands; once made into fine and coarse葛 cloth, her feelings were deep in cherishing and sparing them. Rubbing clean the soiled and rinsing the worn—not that she lacked the splendor of patterned damask, yet every thread and filament came wholly from the work of her own warp and woof. Attending upon her lord, she followed him in dignified ceremonial robes; setting right the people of the state, they looked toward her transforming influence like pure white silk taking dye. "Admirable indeed! The enterprise that laid the foundation"—only Ji Zha 季札 alone perceived its depth; "vast and overflowing! The music that fills the ears"—if not for Music Master Zhi 師摯, who could have sounded forth its splendor? Since the continuation of that virtuous renown grew distant, one sighs that such pure excellence was no longer proclaimed. The licentious airs of Zheng were intermittently performed within the inner chambers, while the New Discourses (Xinyu) were praised beforehand from horseback. Once the palace norms had fallen into ruin, Kuang Heng's 匡衡 forthright memorials were laboured in vain; when the ruler's will had already grown dissipated, what avail was it to expound the Classics beside the Taiye Pool? All these were cases where words were spoken yet not suited to practical use, which also came from those scholars not having met with the right time in their lives. Reverently I reflect that Your Majesty [〇〇〇〇], whose supreme virtue is abyssal and subtle, and whose great norms are ordered in due sequence, cultivates filial thoughts without fail, and cautiously attends to the Mandate of Heaven at the subtle incipient moment. …

translation_en: …Withdrawing from the main halls to examine Your own person, You curtail the allowances for imperial attire and delicacies; inquiring into the people's hardships in the informal courts, You relax the levies of merchant string-taxes and liquor monopolies. While Your gracious bounty has already spread throughout the alleys and villages, Your pursuit of learning grows ever more diligent beneath the felt canopies of the lecture halls. Gathering the erudite scholars to discourse upon the Way, You have charged this humble servant with expounding the Odes (Shi)—not merely as a source of delightful amusement, but in reliance upon the benefit of enriching Your mind. Yet I, Your servant, stand ashamed as though facing a wall, and blush at having learned so little from family instruction; my rote skill at scanning texts is easily exhausted, so what counsel worthy of presentation can I possess? Nevertheless, when words are near at hand yet their meaning is far-reaching, their principles await elucidation; how much more so when Heaven is high yet hears what is lowly—how could my exposition be permitted to remain vague and hollow? Having just immersed myself in the texts and gained some insight, it is fitting that I set it forth repeatedly and in depth. Thus I trace the foundation of the royal enterprise of the House of Zhou from Houji onward, and examine the cultivation of women's duties in the inner court from Taijiang downward. Their lords and their wives, cherishing their livelihood with sighs and exclamations, vividly carried on the family traditions; works like the "Airs of Bin" (Binfeng) and "Against Luxurious Ease" (Wuyi), valuing the affairs of the people with vigilant diligence and anxious toil, shared a single continuous fountainhead of the mind. When it came to the time when "women had no public duties, leaving their silkworms and weaving," once that industry ceased, who indeed formed the steps to ruin that brought about the repeated depredations of the Quanrong? Rise and decline have their origins, rooted in the first stirrings of a single thought of reverence or indulgence; order and chaos are never fixed, truly serving as a mirror of survival and destruction for a thousand ages. Having opened the subject and thus completed my explanation, I merely exhaust the humble offerings of a grass-cutter; hoping that what is deemed good in words may be seen in action, I venture to sully Your Majesty's pendant beads and ear-plugs. Husbands plowing and wives weaving—without the trouble of painting pictures, one captures their very likeness; the blind musicians reciting and the sightless…

translation_en:
…chanting, truly through sounds alone can one connect with the way of governance. Unless Your Majesty knows hardship and knows fear, how could You cast aside extravagance and excess? I humbly pray that Your Majesty will strive for radiant and continuous learning, and keep a cautious and diligent mind; look upon the perils of the common people with compassionate relief, and dwell on the Heavenly Throne while remaining mindful of danger; reduce annual tribute demands and abolish equitable transport schemes, settling the living souls in rest and nourishment; distinguish the loyal from the sycophantic and make likes and dislikes impartial, restraining emotions and nature within centrality and harmony; rectify Your own person and rectify the imperial household, drawing out the meaning of "having no depraved thoughts" from the Odes of Lu (Lu song); and divine the years and generations, prolonging the enduring rule of the righteous Zhou capital. Your servant, overwhelmed with looking up to Heaven and gazing upon the Sage in utmost earnestness and trepidation, respectfully presents this memorial for the imperial perusal.

同考試官訓導王批：開創事跡，稽述詳明。至揚厲陳悃，尤見忠義懇然，都人士計當大用者。

夫躬締造之艱，而以焦勞餘慮詒萬世之統緒者，神聖之謨也；履熙洽之世，而以宵旰先憂求開國之精神者，英誼之軌也。莫
translation_en:
Wang Zhidong 王之棟

Comment by Associate Examiner Assistant Instructor Wang 王: His investigation and account of the deeds of founding the dynasty are detailed and clear. When he rises to forceful exposition and pours out his sincere feelings, one sees all the more an earnest loyalty and righteousness—among the scholars of the capital, he may be reckoned one fit for great employment.

Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Li 李: The achievements of founding and preserving the dynasty, and the anxious care over its hardships, are set forth in his reply with detail and clarity. At the end of the piece, his placing ultimate emphasis upon the Sage Mind reveals all the more a boundless loyalty and devotion. Record it.

Comment by Associate Examiner Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) You 尤: He brings out the difficulties faced by our Sacred Ancestor in founding and preserving the realm in a detailed, clear, and incisive manner, truly sufficient to move the Imperial heart. Moreover, his earnest offering of admonition at the close of the essay reveals all the more an endless loyalty and affection; it is fitting to record and present it to the throne.

Comment by Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Han 韓: His exposition and the sentiments that inspire it fully display his loyal sincerity—it is not merely the excellence of his literary composition. Record it.

Comment by Examiner Left Admonisher Zhu 朱: His elucidation and praise of our Sacred Ancestor's anxious thoughts over hardships from beginning to end are most incisive and to the point. And at the end, his returning to offer counsel on the theme of hardship reveals his loyal earnestness all the more. How could the authorities fail to present it? Let it be presented!

Now, to personally experience the hardships of founding a state, and out of anxious toil and far-reaching concern to bequeath a line of succession for ten thousand generations—this is the counsel of a divine sage. To tread an era of radiant peace and harmony, and yet through tireless toil before dawn and after dusk and preemptive憂慮 [solicitude] to seek the spirit of the dynasty's founding—this is the path of a heroic and righteous ruler. If there is no one…

text:
為之前厥基弗昌莫為之後厥澤弗衍兩
者事殊而心合故能奠安四極而繫國祚
于苞桑也知此則我
聖祖創業之心我
皇上保業之道豈非後先相待而成者哉請恭
繹之以復明問夫創守之難貞觀君臣辯
之詳矣謂創難於守者以出百死得一生
顛沛驚撼不若一統之日暇豫圖也玄齡
之言欲太宗不忘得之之難也謂守難於
===
創者以志狃於宴安而患生於所忽杜微
防漸不若兩陣之交俄頃决也魏徵之言
欲太宗思失之之易也夫二者固各有難
也而愚以為未若創守兼之尤難也夫起
義旗於民間而建無競之偉烈釋戎衣於
馬上而定丕顯之訏謨斯豈一人力所能
兼哉而孰有如我
太祖高皇帝之盛者哉今以創業論之昔成湯
起於七十里武王席三分有二之勢順天

punctuated: 為之前，厥基弗昌；莫為之後，厥澤弗衍。兩者事殊而心合，故能奠安四極，而繫國祚于苞桑也。知此，則我聖祖創業之心，我皇上保業之道，豈非後先相待而成者哉？請恭繹之，以復明問。夫創守之難，貞觀君臣辯之詳矣。謂創難於守者，以出百死得一生，顛沛驚撼，不若一統之日暇豫圖也；玄齡之言，欲太宗不忘得之之難也。謂守難於創者，以志狃於宴安，而患生於所忽，杜微防漸，不若兩陣之交俄頃决也；魏徵之言，欲太宗思失之之易也。夫二者固各有難也，而愚以為未若創守兼之尤難也。夫起義旗於民間，而建無競之偉烈；釋戎衣於馬上，而定丕顯之訏謨，斯豈一人力所能兼哉？而孰有如我太祖高皇帝之盛者哉！今以創業論之：昔成湯起於七十里，武王席三分有二之勢，順天
translation_en:
…preceded it, its foundation would not have flourished; had none succeeded it, its blessings would not have been extended. Though the two tasks differ, their minds are united; thus they can pacify the four corners of the world and bind the dynasty's fortune to the sturdy roots of the mulberry. Understanding this, are not the mind with which our Sacred Ancestor founded the enterprise and the Way by which Your Majesty preserves it mutually dependent across time for their completion? Allow me to respectfully elaborate on this in reply to the brilliant question.

As for the relative difficulty of founding and preserving, the sovereign and ministers of the Zhenguan era (627–649) debated it in detail. The argument that founding is more difficult than preserving holds that emerging with one life from a hundred deaths amid upheaval and terror is unlike the leisurely planning of an era of unification; Fang Xuanling's (房玄齡) words were intended to make Emperor Taizong not forget the difficulty of winning the empire. The argument that preserving is more difficult than founding holds that when the will grows accustomed to peace and comfort, disaster arises from neglect, and nipping subtle dangers in the bud is unlike deciding victory in an instant when two battle lines clash; Wei Zheng's (魏徵) words were intended to make Emperor Taizong reflect on the ease of losing it.

Now, both certainly have their own difficulties, yet I humbly consider that neither is as difficult as combining both founding and preserving! Raising the righteous banner among the common people to establish matchless, magnificent achievements, and then shedding armor from horseback to establish illustrious, far-reaching plans—how could this be within the capacity of a single person to combine? Yet who has ever matched the grandeur of our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu, r. 1368–1398)! Now, to speak of founding the enterprise: in antiquity, Cheng Tang (成湯) arose from a territory of seventy li, and King Wu (武王) relied on the advantage of possessing two-thirds of the realm; complying with Heaven…

走擴廓定閩廣盪梁蜀彼獨一項羽易與
===
矣東盡海島西極玉門南編交趾北控榆
朔彼猶病南越匈奴者弗論矣故創業獨
難而肇基最鉅卽漢高讓功也至其創而
兼守則又非他主可望者成湯之世風制
簡質武王末受命禮樂之事徼周公相成
后弗備也漢高不事詩書正朔服色曆文
景始易也唐高僅除苛政典章文物則貞
觀所修也藝祖雖右文而少威靈稅糧諸
法亦與國所定也古今獨周制不可槩
punctuated: 應人，而諸侯景附，皆上世焉之地也；晉陽千里，唐高坐而擁之，竇、王、蕭、劉非敵也；宋藝祖因業於周，孟、李易鞭箠也。獨漢高以亭長起豐、沛，與西楚百戰，平一海內，稱最難耳。我聖祖龍興濠、泗，起布衣有天下，略與漢同，而功實過之。洗九十載胡元之腥穢，復自古帝王之衣冠，彼誅無道秦者，蔑如矣；馘張、陳，走擴廓，定閩、廣，盪梁、蜀，彼獨一項羽，易與矣；東盡海島，西極玉門，南編交趾，北控榆、朔，彼猶病南越、匈奴者，弗論矣。故創業獨難，而肇基最鉅，即漢高讓功也。至其創而兼守，則又非他主可望者。成湯之世，風制簡質；武王末受命，禮樂之事，微周公相成后，弗備也；漢高不事《詩》、《書》，正朔、服色，歷文、景始易也；唐高僅除苛政，典章、文物，則貞觀所修也；藝祖雖右文，而少威靈，稅稂諸法，亦興國所定也。古今獨周制不可及云，
translation_en:
…and responded to men, with the feudal lords rallying to them like shadows, both relied on foundations laid by earlier generations [? 焉之地]. With a thousand li around Jinyang, Emperor Gaozu of Tang sat in possession of it, and Dou [Jiande], Wang [Shichong], Xiao [Xian], and Liu [Wuzhou] were no match for him. The Founding Ancestor of Song (Emperor Taizu) built upon the enterprise of the [Later] Zhou, and the Meng [of Later Shu] and Li [of Southern Tang] were easily whipped into submission. Only Emperor Gaozu of Han, rising from Precinct Head in Feng and Pei, fought a hundred battles against Western Chu to pacify and unify all within the seas; this is acclaimed as the most difficult of all.

Our Sacred Ancestor rose like a dragon from Hao and Si, emerging as a commoner to possess all under Heaven. His rise was broadly similar to that of Han, yet his achievements truly surpassed it. He washed away ninety years of the foul filth of the barbarian Yuan and restored the robes and caps of the emperors and kings of antiquity—compared to this, punishing the unprincipled Qin was nothing! He took the heads of Zhang [Shicheng] and Chen [Youliang], put Köke Temür (Kuokuo) to flight, pacified Min (Fujian) and Guang (Guangdong and Guangxi), and swept clean Liang and Shu (Sichuan)—compared to this, facing only a single Xiang Yu was easy to deal with! To the east, his realm reached the islands of the sea; to the west, it extended as far as the Yumen Pass; to the south, it registered Jiaozhi; and to the north, it commanded Yulin and Shuofang—compared to this, he who was still troubled by Southern Yue (Nanyue) and the Xiongnu is not worth mentioning! Therefore, his founding of the enterprise was uniquely difficult and the foundation he laid was the grandest; even Emperor Gaozu of Han must yield to him in merit.

As for his combining founding with preservation, that again is something no other ruler could hope to match. In the age of Cheng Tang, customs and institutions were simple and unadorned. King Wu received the Mandate late in life, and in matters of rites and music, had it not been for the Duke of Zhou assisting the accomplished sovereign (King Cheng), they would not have been complete. Emperor Gaozu of Han did not occupy himself with the Book of Odes (Shi) and Book of Documents (Shu), and the calendar and colors of vestments were only altered after the reigns of Emperors Wen and Jing. Emperor Gaozu of Tang merely abolished harsh governance, while institutional charters and cultural ordinances were compiled during the Zhenguan reign. And although the Founding Ancestor of Song favored civil culture, he lacked awe-inspiring majesty, and the various laws on taxation [? 稅稂] were likewise only established during the Taiping Xingguo reign. From antiquity to the present, it is said that only the institutions of the Zhou cannot be equaled,…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
而
聖祖甫偃兵戈輒釐制作崇
郊
廟祀百神考雅樂修節文雖周禮不言精矣置
職掌定賦役立兵制申律令雖周官不言
密矣廣封建爵功臣禮名士檢姦惑雖周
誥不言飭矣故創守兼備而垂統尤鴻卽
周武讓烈也今攷其大體載在
大明日曆而宋濂序之曰規摹宏遠者則謂功
===
高萬古也得國正也獨秉全智也敬天勤
民也家法嚴也軍政有統也繹此而
聖祖開創之勳可略睹也其政要載在
聖政記而濂又序之曰綱舉目備者則謂祀事
嚴戎政肅也大本定大分昭也倖位絕民
志定也申禁令覈實效育人才優前代也
正禮儀去神號嚴宫壺勵忠節剷宿弊也
繹此而
聖祖守成之績可略睹也雖然簡編之所紀錄

punctuated: 而聖祖甫偃兵戈，輒釐制作。崇郊、廟，祀百神，考雅樂，修節文，雖《周禮》不言精矣；置職掌，定賦役，立兵制，申律令，雖《周官》不言密矣；廣封建，爵功臣，禮名士，檢姦惑，雖《周誥》不言飭矣。故創守兼備，而垂統尤鴻，卽周武讓烈也。今攷其大體，載在《大明日曆》，而宋濂序之曰「規摹宏遠」者，則謂功高萬古也，得國正也，獨秉全智也，敬天勤民也，家法嚴也，軍政有統也；繹此而聖祖開創之勳可略睹也。其政要載在《聖政記》，而濂又序之曰「綱舉目備」者，則謂祀事嚴、戎政肅也，大本定、大分昭也，倖位絕、民志定也，申禁令、覈實效、育人才、優前代也，正禮儀、去神號、嚴宫壺、勵忠節、剷宿弊也；繹此而聖祖守成之績可略睹也。雖然，簡編之所紀錄，
translation_en:
Yet as soon as our Sacred Ancestor [Emperor Taizu] laid down arms, he immediately put institutions in order. He revered the suburban sacrifices and the ancestral temple, sacrificed to the hundred spirits, investigated court music, and cultivated ritual forms—even the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli) could not be called more refined. He established official duties, fixed taxes and corvée labor, instituted the military system, and promulgated laws and ordinances—even the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan) could not be called more thorough. He broadened the enfeoffment of princes, ennobled meritorious officials, treated eminent scholars with courtesy, and curbed the wicked and deluded—even the Announcements of Zhou (Zhougao) could not be called more rigorous. Therefore, he combined both founding and preserving, and handed down a particularly grand heritage, such that even King Wu of Zhou would yield to his illustrious achievements.

If we now examine the grand outlines of his rule, they are recorded in the Daily Calendar of the Great Ming (Da Ming rili). In his preface to it, Song Lian 宋濂 described its "vast and far-reaching scale," by which he meant that his merit surpassed all antiquity, that he gained the realm legitimately, that he alone possessed complete wisdom, that he revered Heaven and was diligent toward the people, that his family regulations were strict, and that his military administration had unified command. By reflecting on this, the founding meritorious achievements of our Sacred Ancestor can be seen in outline. The essentials of his governance are recorded in the Record of Sacred Governance (Shengzheng ji). In his preface to that work, Lian again described how "the main principles are upheld and the details are complete," by which he meant that sacrificial affairs were solemn and military administration was disciplined; the great foundation was settled and the great distinctions of status were made clear; undeserved appointments were cut off and the minds of the people were settled; prohibitions and ordinances were promulgated, actual results were verified, men of talent were nurtured, and generous treatment was accorded to the ruling house of the former dynasty; ritual decorum was rectified, improper titles of spirits were removed, the inner palace was strictly regulated, loyalty and integrity were encouraged, and long-standing abuses were eradicated. By reflecting on this, the achievements of our Sacred Ancestor in preserving and consolidating the dynastic enterprise can be seen in outline. Even so, from what is recorded in books and documents…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
故老之所傳誦可以知
聖人之偉績而未可以見
聖人之心
聖人之心非善守成業而深遡其始事之難者
不易知也我
聖祖自起義以至末命其間十載百戰之勞三
紀經營之慮曷嘗一日知黃屋左纛之尊
玉食瓊宮之樂哉至正末造饑疫相仍薄
游汝潁寄泊荆黃空乏拂亂何弗備也旣
===
入滁陽彭趙外挾德崖內掩驪頷虎口何
弗探也及統大軍鄱陽夜圍岳州晝襲風
櫛雨沐何弗嘗也比正
大寶早朝晏罷焦心勞慮爲萬民立命何弗周
也二百禩於茲蓋嘗變於土木訌於齊劉
藍鄢突起於鐇濠警寇於倭虜而長治久
安如金甌無缺覆盂不搖者寔我
聖祖精神之所攝持勤勞之所底定蓋滋遠矣
愚嘗伏讀

punctuated: 故老之所傳誦，可以知聖人之偉績，而未可以見聖人之心。聖人之心，非善守成業而深遡其始事之難者，不易知也。我聖祖自起義以至末命，其間十載百戰之勞，三紀經營之慮，曷嘗一日知黃屋左纛之尊、玉食瓊宮之樂哉！至正末造，饑疫相仍，薄游汝、潁，寄泊荆、黃，空乏拂亂，何弗備也？旣入滁陽，彭、趙外挾，德崖內掩，驪頷虎口，何弗探也？及統大軍，鄱陽夜圍，岳州晝襲，風櫛雨沐，何弗嘗也？比正大寶，早朝晏罷，焦心勞慮，爲萬民立命，何弗周也？二百禩於茲，蓋嘗變於土木，訌於齊、劉、藍、鄢，突起於鐇、濠，警寇於倭、虜，而長治久安，如金甌無缺、覆盂不搖者，寔我聖祖精神之所攝持、勤勞之所底定，蓋滋遠矣。愚嘗伏讀
translation_en: …and what the elders pass down and recite, one can know the Sage's great achievements, yet one cannot perceive the Sage's mind. As for the Sage's mind, unless one is skilled at preserving the established patrimony and deeply traces back the hardships of how the enterprise was begun, it is not easy to understand. From the time our Sacred Ancestor raised a righteous uprising until his final testamentary charge—with the toil of a hundred battles over ten years and the anxieties of thirty-six years of planning and administration in between—when did he ever for a single day know the grandeur of the yellow-canopied carriage and left-mounted feathered standard, or the pleasures of jade-like delicacies and jasper palaces! In the final years of the Zhizheng era (1341–1368), famine and pestilence followed one upon another; he wandered briefly through Ru and Ying and lodged temporarily in Jing and Huang—what destitution and frustration did he not experience to the full? After entering Chuyang, with Peng Zaizhu and Zhao Junyong pressing from without and Sun Deya ambushing from within, what peril under the black dragon's chin or in the tiger's jaws did he not brave? When he came to command the grand armies, with night encirclements at Lake Poyang and daytime raids at Yuezhou, combed by the wind and bathed by the rain, what hardship did he not taste? And when he ascended the Great Treasure, holding court early and retiring late, racking his heart and exhausting his thoughts to establish a secure life for the myriad people, in what respect was he not thorough? In the two hundred years down to the present, there was the disaster at Tumu, internal turmoil from Qi Yanming, Liu Liu, Liu Qi, Lan Tingrui, and Yan Bengshu, sudden uprisings by Zhu Zhifan and Zhu Chenhao, and alarms of raids by Japanese pirates and northern nomads; yet the realm has enjoyed enduring order and lasting peace, like a golden goblet without a flaw or an overturned bowl that cannot be shaken. This is truly because what the spirit of our Sacred Ancestor sustained and what his diligence stabilized has reached ever farther in its effect. I, in my simplicity, have humbly read…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
大宴功臣之諭有曰天下大業以艱難得之
當以艱難守之人情謹憂患忽宴安不知
憂患始於宴安也至哉斯言所望於後之
嗣服者何深切哉我
皇上凝靈含睿宰敬宅虚夙夜遹追仰稽
先烈頃因

郊祭必虔
廟饗必肅穆乎敬天之範也聞災軫傷占象避
殿惕乎勤民之指也戎王稽首餘醜屢殲烈

translation_en:
… His edict at the grand banquet for meritorious officials, which says: "The great enterprise of the empire was won through hardship, and must be preserved through hardship. Human nature is to be cautious in times of distress and negligent in times of ease and comfort, not realizing that distress begins in ease and comfort." How supreme are these words! How profound and earnest is the hope He placed in those who would succeed to the throne in later generations!

Our Emperor concentrates spiritual excellence and harbors sage wisdom, governing with reverence and dwelling in open-mindedness; from dawn to night He follows His forebears' footsteps, looking up to examine their illustrious achievements. Recently, in the course of lectures and readings on the Ancestral Injunctions and Veritable Records (Zuzong xunlu), He first singled out the compilation on the Hardships of Founding the Dynasty (Chuangye jiannan), going over it again and again and drawing out its meaning, unable to bear putting down the scroll. He may truly be said to skillfully carry on the intentions of our Sacred Ancestor!

Therefore, the suburban sacrifices are unfailingly devout and the ancestral temple offerings unfailingly solemn—how august is this model of revering Heaven! Upon hearing of disasters He is moved with compassion, and upon observing celestial portents He withdraws from the main hall—how vigilant is this aim of laboring for the people! The chieftains of the western戎 (Rong) bow their heads to the ground, and the remaining miscreants are repeatedly annihilated—how glorious is this merit of maintaining military readiness! Empty formalities are unfailingly dispelled, and fraudulent abuses are all halted—how strict is this rule of verifying realities! All of these are magnificent deeds of emulating the Ancestors.

Yet you, sir, still wish to stoop to gather humble offerings like wild celery and basking in the sun—what, then, can I present? In my humble opinion, the territory of the empire cannot be further expanded, rites and music cannot be further cultivated, and institutional systems cannot be made more detailed. Even if there are partial omissions that are not carried out, or deteriorated practices that ought to be rectified, the two…

成憲在焉一補捄之足矣語曰作者心勞因者

在

非難矣思創制立法之勞孰與重熈累洽
之安而尚謂盈縮紀綱整齊法度爲難乎
非難矣所謂守成之難者謂不知創業之
難故難也知創業之難則弗難矣
聖天子早夜圖難故愚敢以艱難之說進進艱
難之說安敢忌諱焉惟執事實重圖之
第二問
申用懋
punctuated:
百年成憲在焉，一補捄之足矣。語曰：「作者心勞，因者功半。」是無用艱難爲也。乃若艱難則有之，在聖心而已矣。思汝、潁、荊、黃之阨，孰與穆清廣大之安？而尚謂不邇聲色、不殖貨利爲難乎？非難矣。思彭、趙、德崖之急，孰與臣妾億兆之安？而尚謂霽威受諫、側席待理爲難乎？非難矣。思櫛風沐雨之苦，孰與父天母地之安？而尚謂敬天勤民、輕徭薄賦爲難乎？非難矣。思創制立法之勞，孰與重熙累洽之安？而尚謂盈縮紀綱、整齊法度爲難乎？非難矣。所謂守成之難者，謂不知創業之難，故難也；知創業之難，則弗難矣。聖天子早夜圖難，故愚敢以艱難之說進。進艱難之說，安敢忌諱焉？惟執事實重圖之。

第二問
申用懋
translation_en:
…hundred years of established institutions are right there; simply patching and remedying them will suffice. As the saying goes: "The creator toils in mind; the successor achieves results with half the effort." Thus there is no need to make a hardship of it. Yet where hardship does exist, it lies solely within the sacred mind of the Emperor.

If one reflects on the perils at Ru, Ying, Jing, and Huang, how do they compare with the peace of serene and vast majesty? Could one then still consider it difficult to stay aloof from sensual pleasures and refrain from amassing wealth and profit? It is not difficult. If one reflects on the crises involving Peng, Zhao, and Sun Deya, how do they compare with the peace of ruling over millions of subjects? Could one then still consider it difficult to soften one's majesty to accept remonstrance and to sit attentively awaiting good governance? It is not difficult. If one reflects on the bitterness of being combed by the wind and bathed by the rain, how does it compare with the peace of having Heaven as father and Earth as mother? Could one then still consider it difficult to revere Heaven, labor for the people, and lighten corvée and reduce taxes? It is not difficult. If one reflects on the toil of creating institutions and establishing laws, how does it compare with the peace of cumulative prosperity and harmony across generations? Could one then still consider it difficult to adjust the纲纪 [guiding principles of state] and regulate the laws and institutions? It is not difficult.

What is called the difficulty of preserving what has been achieved is difficult only because one does not know the difficulty of founding the enterprise; once one knows the difficulty of founding the enterprise, then it is no longer difficult. Because the sacred Son of Heaven plans for difficulties from morning to night, I dare to present this discourse on hardship. In presenting a discourse on hardship, how could I dare to avoid taboo subjects? May Your Excellency give it serious consideration.

Second Policy Question
Shen Yongmao 申用懋

This essay examines and verifies in thorough detail the responses of calamities and auspicious omens since antiquity; truly its discourse flows with coherence and grace. At the end, the candidate further offers three proposals—he must be one who has long harbored loyal sincerity. This should be recorded for publication as an aid to His Majesty in reaching and moving Heaven.

Within the essay, he further speaks with impassioned urgency regarding current affairs; the way of moral cultivation and self-examination is fully set forth here. It should be recorded for presentation to the throne.

Examiner, Expositor-in-waiting Han, comments: In discussing the interaction between Heaven and man, his detailed analysis is precise and accurate, and what moves him to sigh with deep feeling is relevant and incisive, showing all the more his loyal devotion. A fine scholar, a fine scholar!

Examiner, Left Admonisher Zhu, comments: Most people are able to repeat the standard theories of calamities and auspicious omens; you alone synthesize antiquity and take measure of the present, penetratingly discerning the causes of order and disorder. You are one who has truly devoted his mind to the study of Heaven and man.

Now, when a true king rides the ascendant fortune of yang and unifies the six directions of the cosmos, how could even the slightest subtlety fail to be connected with Heaven? Therefore, when pure reverence spreads and reaches on high, and auspicious omens all manifest themselves, this is the tally of Heaven blessing those who are compliant; when idle pleasure grows great, and disasters and anomalies variously appear, this is the majesty of Heaven punishing excess. As for slight faults committed in secluded solitude, celestial phenomena and terrestrial forms send down warnings of blame; when great peace has just begun, disharmonious qi occasionally gives a sign. For Heaven illuminates even the most minute and hidden things in order to admonish for the future; its concern lies in times of abundance and prosperity, warning against how easily fullness tips over. text:
之軌廣平康之猷闡補救之術諸福已備
而焦勞弗休微孽未萌而宵旰必厲故能
感召太和凝承靈貺鞏有道之長而臻上
治之極也愚生於天人之際弗達也顧執
事明問所及卽臆說敢不盡對夫說天莫
精於易在大有曰天祐剝曰天行賁曰觀
天文察時變夬曰有隕自天則虧益之宰
欽若之義斡旋之效備矣稽休咎莫辨於

punctuated:
之軌，廣平康之猷，闡補救之術，諸福已備而焦勞弗休，微孽未萌而宵旰必厲，故能感召太和，凝承靈貺，鞏有道之長而臻上治之極也。愚生於天人之際弗達也，顧執事明問所及，卽臆說敢不盡對？
夫說天莫精於《易》。在〈大有〉曰「天祐」，〈剝〉曰「天行」，〈賁〉曰「觀天文，察時變」，〈夬〉曰「有隕自天」，則虧益之宰、欽若之義、斡旋之效備矣。稽休咎莫辨於《書》。曰「肅、乂、哲、謀、聖，而庶徵時若」，曰「狂、僭、豫、蒙、急，而庶徵恒若」，則感通之理彰矣。陳謹畏莫著於《詩》。于〈板〉則「無敢戲豫，無敢馳驅」，于〈雲漢〉則「敬恭明神，宜無悔怒」，其勅幾之旨切矣。述鑒戒莫詳於《春秋》。曰日食、曰不雨、曰螟蜮，必累書；曰隕、曰震、曰饑、曰孛彗，必特書，其儆省之意深矣。繇斯以觀，天以災祥示人昭昭也。
後世陰陽家占應之說，雖泥而中者什七。如三川震而周遷，客星見而晉禍，皆符於數而不可不存也。禳除
translation_en:
…path of simplicity and economy, broaden plans for peace and tranquility, and expound methods of remediation. Even when all blessings are already complete, they do not cease their anxious toil; even before minor portents of evil have sprouted, they unfailingly redouble their diligence from dawn to dusk. Thus they are able to summon Supreme Harmony, consolidate and receive divine favor, secure the longevity of a righteous reign, and reach the pinnacle of supreme governance. As a foolish student, I do not fully comprehend the correlation between Heaven and man; yet regarding what Your Excellency has touched upon in your enlightened inquiry, even with my mere conjectures, how dare I not reply in full?

Now, in explaining Heaven, nothing is more subtle than the Classic of Changes (Yi). Under the hexagram Dayou ("Great Possession") it speaks of "Heaven's aid"; under Bo ("Splitting Apart"), "the movement of Heaven"; under Bi ("Grace"), "observing the patterns of Heaven to examine the changes of the seasons"; and under Guai ("Breakthrough"), "something falling from Heaven." Thus the sovereign principle of diminution and increase, the duty of reverent accord, and the efficacy of turning fate around are all fully set forth therein. In examining auspicious and inauspicious signs, nothing is more discerning than the Classic of Documents (Shu). It says, "Solemnity, orderliness, wisdom, deliberation, and sageliness—and the various verifications are timely," and it says, "Wildness, presumption,indolence, rashness [?], and haste—and the various verifications are constant." Thus the principle of mutual resonance and response is made manifest. In setting forth caution and awe, nothing is clearer than the Classic of Odes (Shi). In the ode "Ban" it says, "Dare not jest or take your ease, dare not驰驅 (gallop wildly about)"; in the ode "Yunhan" ("The Milky Way") it says, "We have reverently honored the bright spirits; they ought to hold no lingering anger." Its purport of admonishing at the subtleincipience of things is earnest indeed. In recounting warnings and admonitions, nothing is more detailed than the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu). Eclipses of the sun, lack of rain, and plagues of locusts and grain-pests are invariably recorded repeatedly; falling stars or stones, earthquakes, famines, and comets are invariably given special record. Its intent to warn and prompt self-reflection is profound. Viewed in this light, it is crystal clear that Heaven instructs mankind through calamities and auspicious prodigies.

In later ages, although the theories of divination and verification advanced by the Naturalists (Yinyang jia) were overly rigid, they hit the mark seven times out of ten. For instance, when the Three Rivers quaked and the Zhou moved its capital, or when a guest star appeared and disaster befell the Jin—all such events corresponded to fate's regularities and cannot be dismissed. As for rituals of propitiation and exorcism…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之議雖淺而應者亦屢如文仲之減食省
用也以消旱晏子之諫臺池誅戮也以去
彗皆正於事而不可不考也然使人主徇
數而核其所中是遇祲而修其修易惰緣
事而強其所應是執一而備其備易疎要
在旁括古今之變總覽理亂之原潜析敬
怠之塗上徹冲冥之奧乃知祥以符德其
反也導驕災以告怒其竟也玉成雖乗牒
浩繁更僕難數而槩可論已故日有五色
===
瑞也金天以興劉昱以廢五星聚宿瑞也
姬運以恢天寶以亂甘露潤矣將唐之元
和媲美陶唐乎嘉禾九穗矣豈晉之太康
比迹周成乎貞觀永徽之政懸矣而均奏
河清軒轅元狩之世異矣而並稱麟見亢
暘失衆之應也辛以斬祚湯則永命流星
破軍之兆也晉以始難光武一統狐升座
而炎滅雉呴鼎而中興莫非羽孽也芝産
殿而唐警桑大拱而殷治莫非木妖也夫

punctuated: 之議雖淺，而應者亦屢。如文仲之減食省用也以消旱，晏子之諫臺池誅戮也以去彗，皆正於事而不可不考也。然使人主徇數而核其所中，是遇祲而修，其修易惰；緣事而強其所應，是執一而備，其備易疎。要在旁括古今之變，總覽理亂之原，潜析敬怠之塗，上徹冲冥之奧，乃知祥以符德，其反也導驕；災以告怒，其竟也玉成。雖乗牒浩繁，更僕難數，而槩可論已。故日有五色，瑞也，金天以興，劉昱以廢；五星聚宿，瑞也，姬運以恢，天寶以亂。甘露潤矣，將唐之元和媲美陶唐乎？嘉禾九穗矣，豈晉之太康比迹周成乎？貞觀、永徽之政懸矣，而均奏河清；軒轅、元狩之世異矣，而並稱麟見。亢暘，失衆之應也，辛以斬祚，湯則永命；流星，破軍之兆也，晉以始難，光武一統。狐升座而炎滅，雉呴鼎而中興，莫非羽孽也；芝産殿而唐警，桑大拱而殷治，莫非木妖也。夫
translation_en:
… rituals are shallow, yet they too have repeatedly proven effective. For instance,臧 Wenzhong’s (Zang Wenzhong 臧文仲) reducing food and economizing on expenditures in order to dispel a drought, and Master Yan’s (Yanzi 晏子) remonstrating against terraces, ponds, and executions in order to make a comet disappear—all were rectifications applied to actual affairs and cannot go unexamined. Yet if a ruler merely follows numerical prognostications to verify what hits the mark, he will cultivate himself only when encountering an ominous portent, and such cultivation easily lapses into indolence; if he merely latches onto specific affairs to force a corresponding response, he will cling to a single measure in making preparations, and such preparations easily become lax. The essential point lies in broadly encompassing the transformations of past and present, comprehensively surveying the origins of order and disorder, deeply analyzing the paths of reverence and negligence, and penetrating upward into the mysteries of the profound and unseen. Only then will one understand that while auspicious signs correspond to virtue, their opposite effect is to induce arrogance; and while calamities announce Heaven’s wrath, their ultimate outcome is to polish and bring one to perfection. Although the historical records are vast and too numerous to recount even if relays of attendants took turns, their general principles can nonetheless be discussed.

Thus, the sun appearing in five colors is an auspicious sign: Jintian (Shaohao 少昊) rose to prominence by it, whereas Liu Yu 劉昱 (Emperor Houfei of Liu Song) was deposed. The five planets gathering in a single lunar lodge is an auspicious sign: the destiny of the Ji 姬 clan (the Zhou dynasty) was expanded by it, whereas the Tianbao 天寶 reign (of Tang Xuanzong) fell into rebellion. Sweet dew fell moisteningly—yet could the Yuanhe 元和 reign of the Tang rival the glory of Taotang 陶唐 (Emperor Yao)? Auspicious grain bore nine ears on a single stalk—yet how could the Taikang 太康 reign of the Jin match the footsteps of King Cheng of Zhou 周成王? The governance of the Zhenguan 貞觀 (Tang Taizong) and Yonghui 永徽 (Tang Gaozong) reigns differed vastly, yet both reported the Yellow River running clear; the eras of Xuanyuan 軒轅 (the Yellow Emperor) and Yuanshou 元狩 (Han Wudi) were worlds apart, yet both claimed the appearance of a unicorn (lin 麟). Extreme drought is the response to losing the multitude: Dixin 帝辛 (King Zhou of Shang) thereby had his throne cut short, whereas Tang 湯 perpetuated his mandate. A streaking meteor is the omen of a routed army: the Jin dynasty thereby began its troubles, whereas Emperor Guangwu 光武帝 (of the Eastern Han) unified the realm. A wild bird [?] ascended the throne and the Fiery Han (Shu Han 蜀漢, or Western Jin [?]) perished, whereas a pheasant crowed upon a tripod vessel and a dynastic restoration (under Wuding 武丁 of Shang) was achieved—yet both were avian anomalies (yunie 羽孽). Glossy ganoderma (zhi 芝) grew in the palace hall and the Tang took warning, whereas a mulberry tree grew to two-handed girth in the court and the Yin (Shang) achieved order—yet both were botanical prodigies (muyao 木妖). title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
數君者同機異應較若霄壤少昊黃帝神
堯周文皆最盛德矣而成王雖幼守成之
哲后也太宗雖覇納諫之明主也故能享
有佳禎臻厥茂祜彼遴耗海內驕平吳宜
鮮終矣鳴牝雞迎佛骨宜不振矣寵僧智
任林甫宜喪敗矣何恠乎祥之不盡為祥
也斯非天驕之而自驕也成湯懋德猶省
六事美哉時忱矣而受伊陟之戒行祖己
之訓武丁太戊信賢君也齊豁達之度攬
===
三公之權世祖亦誼辟也是以妖不勝善
彌熾以昌彼且淫于長夜制于近習宜身
僇而祚移矣昏極於肉糜意酣于霓裳宜
五胡起而四海兵矣何駭乎災之果能為
災也斯非天殃之而自殃也是故治有治
徵亂有亂象而有不盡爾者定未定之說
也要之君道得則治君道失則亂天曷嘗
不定哉洪惟
向皇帝篤恭凝命首

…these several rulers shared the same omens yet experienced different outcomes, as distinct as heaven and earth. Shaohao, the Yellow Emperor (Huangdi), the divine Yao, and King Wen of Zhou all possessed the most flourishing virtue. And though King Cheng was young, he was a wise sovereign who preserved the accomplishments of his predecessors; though Tang Taizong ruled through hegemonic force, he was an enlightened ruler who accepted remonstrance. Therefore, they were able to enjoy auspicious signs and attain abundant blessings. As for those others—exhausting the realm [like Han Wudi][?] and growing arrogant after pacifying Wu [like Jin Wudi], it was fitting that they rarely came to a good end; allowing the hen to crow at dawn [under Tang Gaozong] and welcoming the Buddha's bone [under Tang Xianzong], it was fitting that they failed to thrive; favoring the monk Zhi [or clerical wisdom][?] and employing Li Linfu [under Tang Xuanzong], it was fitting that they suffered ruin and defeat. What wonder is it that auspicious omens do not always turn out to be auspicious? This is not Heaven making them arrogant, but their making themselves arrogant.

Cheng Tang exerted himself in virtue and still examined himself on six counts—how admirable was his constant sincerity! Receiving the admonitions of Yi Zhi and practicing the instructions of Zu Ji, Wu Ding and Tai Wu were truly worthy rulers; matching a magnanimous breadth of mind and concentrative grasp of the power of the Three Dukes, Shizu [Emperor Guangwu of Han] was likewise a righteous sovereign. Therefore, portents could not overcome goodness, and their dynasties grew ever more flourishing and prosperous. As for those others—indulging in "long nights" of debauchery [like King Zhou of Shang] and being controlled by close favorites [like the late Han emperors], it was fitting that their persons were slain and their thrones passed to others; reaching the utmost stupidity of suggesting "minced meat porridge" [like Jin Huidi] and becoming intoxicated with the "Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Coat" dance [like Tang Xuanzong], it was fitting that the Five Barbarians (Wu Hu) rose up and all within the Four Seas was plunged into war. Why be startled that calamities indeed prove to be calamities? This is not Heaven bringing disaster upon them, but their bringing disaster upon themselves.

Therefore, order has the signs of order, and chaos has the portents of chaos; yet the fact that it is not always completely so is explained by the theory of Heaven being "settled or not yet settled." In sum, when the Way of the Ruler is attained, there is order; when the Way of the Ruler is lost, there is chaos—how could Heaven ever be unsettled?

Vast indeed was our late Emperor [? 向皇帝, likely a transcription error for 高皇帝, Emperor Gao, or 先皇帝, the late Emperor], who with steadfast reverence consolidated the Mandate, and first…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
諭天下臣民毋言祥瑞諸有災異毋匿不聞於
是五星合而求直言中原水而贖鬻子免
租之
詔歲出賑恤之
令四頒故三十年間雖彗見者五客犯者三太
白熒惑之經六水旱螽螟之異時有而
大統昭垂卜世無極蓋敬勤之效章章已我
皇上恭纂
熈業尤肅小心往者星變而董百官河決而諮
===
羣議近則江淮南北告饑減田租出帑金
責有司奉行必以實而雨暘失時輒廑
露禱日月薄蝕必肅
齋修弭災迎祥之意甚盛宜夫天無蘊寶地
有呈祥以昭靈貺徵順助也而何西北攙
槍邊陲流火都城大癘三輔旱霾頃則巨
浸漂邑訛言驚眾者所在又見告矣將氣
有舛順而適與數合哉抑天故有告譴歟
理所未解宜執事諄諄問也愚何知試以

translation_en:
…instructed all officials and subjects under Heaven not to speak of auspicious omens, and whenever there were natural disasters or anomalies, not to conceal them or fail to report them. Thus, when the five planets converged, he sought forthright counsel; when the Central Plains suffered floods, he redeemed children who had been sold; edicts remitting taxes were issued every year, and orders for famine relief were promulgated in all directions. Therefore, over the course of thirty years, although comets appeared five times, guest stars trespassed thrice, Venus and Mars crossed the sky in daylight or violated constellations six times, and anomalies of flood, drought, and locusts occurred from time to time, yet the Great Line was gloriously handed down and the divination of the dynasty's generations was boundless—truly, the efficacy of reverence and diligence was manifest indeed!

Our Emperor has reverently succeeded to the radiant enterprise and is even more solemn and circumspect. In the past, when celestial anomalies occurred, he admonished the hundred officials, and when the Yellow River breached its banks, he consulted the deliberations of the court; recently, when famine was reported north and south of the Yangtze and Huai rivers, he reduced land taxes, disbursed treasury funds, and charged the authorities to carry out relief measures with genuine substance. Moreover, whenever rain and sunshine are out of season, he is invariably moved to pray in the open air; whenever the sun or moon is eclipsed, he unfailingly observes solemn fasts and self-cultivation. His intention to avert disasters and welcome auspiciousness is most abundant. One would expect Heaven to withhold no precious blessings and Earth to present auspicious signs, so as to manifest divine favor and attest to harmonious assistance.

Why, then, have there been comets in the northwest, shooting stars on the frontiers, a great pestilence in the capital, and drought and dust storms in the metropolitan region, while just recently great floods submerging towns and false rumors alarming the populace have again been reported everywhere? Is it that cosmic ether has its aberrations and harmonies, which happen to coincide with fate? Or is it that Heaven is deliberately issuing warnings and reprimands? This principle is difficult to comprehend, so it is fitting that Your Excellency earnestly inquiries into it. What does this ignorant candidate know? Yet I shall venture to…

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
三說獻蓋聞曰應天以實不以文今
朝政無闕矣然六府三事果盡修歟吏不墮
窳歟士不虛憍歟囹圄空歟卒旅奮歟潢
池無嘯歟老有年而稚無殤歟有一於斯
皆謂蠹治即減膳徹樂爲文而已矣必也
去彌飾而舉功實省議論而重責成則實
政也蓋聞曰奉天在於修德戒謹尚於未
形今
聖衷信翼翼矣不曰翠微玉華箴規隔乎內恬
===

賞予易濫乎土木易興乎有一於斯皆謂
侮衷即省躬避殿爲暫而已矣必也防衆
欲而謹獨知隄未萌而戒先事則豫道也
昔桓公聞貴天而仰視管仲曰天非蒼蒼
之天也人主以百姓爲天今遐邇誠向戴
矣乃遼代困虜趙魏困盜淮泗困河周衛
困歲吳越困催科閩廣滇粵困雜夷夫匹

translation_en:
…present three arguments. For I have heard it said: "Respond to Heaven with substance, not with mere formality." Today the court's governance is without deficiency; yet are the Six Treasuries and Three Businesses truly all in good order? Are the officials free from indolence and neglect? Are the literati free from empty arrogance? Are the prisons empty? Are the troops and armies roused with vigor? Are there no bandits whistling in the marshes [lit. "the pools"]? Do the elderly enjoy their full years and the young avoid premature death? If even one of these fails, it is called an erosion of governance—and then reducing the imperial table or suspending court music is nothing more than mere formality. Only by casting aside superficial gloss to promote substantive achievement, and curtailing empty debate to emphasize accountability for results, can there be substantive governance.

I have also heard it said: "Serving Heaven lies in cultivating virtue, and caution and reverence value acting before things take form." Today the Sacred Mind is truly reverent and circumspect; yet might it not be said that in the Cuiwei and Yuhua palaces, remonstrance and admonition are cut off? That with tranquility inside and peace outside, ease and pleasure gradually creep in? That petitions through palace women easily flourish? That personal tastes and desires easily grow miscellaneous? That rewards and grants easily become lavish? That construction projects easily arise? If even one of these occurs, it is called a slight to one's inner sincerity—and then self-examination or vacating the main hall is nothing more than a temporary gesture. Only by guarding against the multitude of desires and being watchful over what is known to oneself alone, diking up what has not yet sprouted and taking warning before events occur, can one attain the Way of preparedness.

In antiquity, when Duke Huan [of Qi] heard the words "value Heaven," he looked up at the sky. Guan Zhong (管仲) said: "Heaven is not the蒼蒼 [vast blue] sky above; the ruler of men takes the common people as his Heaven." Today those far and near truly turn toward and revere the throne; yet Liao and Dai are distressed by northern caitiffs, Zhao and Wei are distressed by bandits, the Huai and Si regions are distressed by the Yellow River, Zhou and Wei are distressed by bad harvests, Wu and Yue are distressed by tax collection, and Fujian, Guangdong, Yunnan, and Guangxi are distressed by various non-Chinese tribes. Now, a single ordinary man or woman can still move Heaven to send down frost or bring about drought—how much more so thehundreds of millions of people! Only…

… [It must be] as if driving with rotten reins, feeling the people's pain and distress in one's own person, dwelling on high while commiserating with those living in nests and caves, and dining on jade-like delicacies while remembering those who eat coarse grain and parched meal—this is the way to honor Heaven. By cultivating these three things, and with the Son of Heaven further investigating antiquity and rectifying learning, accepting admonition and drawing close to the worthy, unravelling the waxing and waning in the Book of Changes (Zhouyi), examining the auspicious and inauspicious signs in the "Great Plan" ("Hongfan"), observing the manifest warnings of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Linjing), chanting the verses set forth in the Odes of Zhou (Zhouya), practicing this with continuous brightness, and carrying it on with cautious diligence—then the hundred spirits will accept their duties, the myriad numina will bestow their discerning gaze, and how could any calamity possibly arise? Theories of divination and portents and proposals for exorcism and lustration are truly rigid and shallow; there is no need to discuss them.

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
鑒戒此作得之矣
考試官左諭德朱　批　論諸史甚精確至謂無
關君德治道史無益也意深哉異日當為良史矣
聖人以心存天下萬世而慮之也至聖人
以道維天下萬世而律之也嚴惟其慮之
至故不得不以勸懲寄之文惟其律之嚴
故所寄勸懲于文者必至當而不易嗟乎
聖人所筆削之史固其以道律天下萬世
而寄其心于不窮者也故不謂之史而謂
===

… as a mirror and warning for the world, this piece has grasped it.
Examiner Zhu, Left Admonisher (Zuo yude), comments: Its discussion of the various histories is exceedingly precise and accurate. When it comes to saying that if a work has no bearing on the ruler's virtue or the way of governance, then history is of no benefit—how profound is its meaning! In the future, the author will surely make a fine historian.

The sage preserves All-under-Heaven and ten thousand generations in his mind, and his concern for them is utmost; the sage upholds All-under-Heaven and ten thousand generations with the Way, and his regulation of them is strict. Precisely because his concern is utmost, he cannot but entrust encouragement and warning to writing; precisely because his regulation is strict, the encouragement and warning that he entrusts to writing must be supremely fitting and immutable. Alas! The history written and edited by the sage is indeed that whereby he regulates All-under-Heaven and ten thousand generations with the Way and entrusts his mind to eternity; therefore it is not called a history, but is called a Classic. When scholars read the Classic of the sage so as to probe his mind and the Way, only then can they evaluate the histories of later ages, which does not lie merely in petty matters of wording. Allow me to reply to the discerning question with this.

Ever since knotted cords were replaced, the Classics and histories have shared a single source. The Four Historians originated in the era of the sovereigns, and the Five Historians were established under the苍籙 [Azure Register, i.e., in remote antiquity]. The Right recorded words and the Left recorded deeds, with officials devoting their lives to their profession; the Celestial Official and the Grand Historian transmitted their learning from generation to generation within their families. Every movement of the ruler had to be written down: great matters were recorded on bamboo tablets (ce), small matters on wooden slips and boards (jiandu), and each year had its compilation—there were no two distinct forms. At the height of this practice, Yu could not praise Gun, Guan and Cai could not disparage the Duke of Zhou, Zhao Dun could not alter the brush of Dong Hu, and the Cui clan could not seize away the bamboo slips of the Historian of the South (Nanshi). In sum, public justice was manifest and encouragement and warning were clearly displayed, nothing more. When the virtue of Zhou declined, Confucius …

title: 萬曆十年順天府鄉試錄
text:
子傷乾綱之解紐睹王跡之久熄既為之
賛易叙書修禮刪詩以明道矣猶以為徒
託空言不若見諸行事者為足以律天下
萬世也而春秋作焉假二百四十二年南
面之權賞罰天下以存王法故春秋者史
之經道之用也蘇明允曰經以道法勝史
以事辭勝要之不可偏廢焉顧史無定體
而作者二之後世之睹編年則自左丘明
始矣志本周公事傳孔筆或先經以始事
===
或後經以終義或依經以辨理或錯經以
合異名之曰左氏傳其為例也微而顯志
而晦婉而成章盡而不汗懲惡而勸善自
有書契以來蔚乎稱品藻矣夫仲尼素王
丘明素臣道法淵源豈以文掩乎斯其上
也後世之睹傳紀者則自司馬遷始矣創
新義例解散編年作書以載制度作表以
紀歲月作紀以明統系作傳以著賢否名
曰史記其序事也辨而不華質而不俚其
